frame, forcing the bridge to close even after the pipeline had already fenced

offline recovery tests passed 2/2 with local MCP subprocess IPC; Ruff passed.

provider readiness. Next laptop sequence should verify error → next command on
the same session before broad routing trials.

## Implemented components and reasoning

- contracts.py validates bounded PCM16/16 kHz mono audio and session/turn keys.
- servers.py and speech.py implement separate ASR/TTS MCP stdio processes, typed schemas, ordered incremental input/partial/final ASR, pull TTS, operation leases, deadlines, cancellation and cleanup. Final-only providers can use an explicitly buffered fallback. This avoids adding an auxiliary channel before measurement justifies it. Per-chunk JSON/base64 overhead is still a Pi gate.
- providers.py defines incremental ASR, closable reasoning/TTS streams and typed tool calls with deterministic mocks. configuration.py selects documented role/protocol adapters from remote.py and gates live execution on explicit authorization, request bounds and project credentials. These adapters have only offline contract verification. The old ElevenLabs prototype is excluded from runtime selection and remains fake-transport-only. Mock TTS produces tones, not speech.
- audio.py supplies strict WAV format/length checks, actual CPU Silero, 320 ms pre-roll, provisional 640 ms endpoint silence and a 30-second cap. Connected replay supports actual configured Sherpa wake or an explicitly labelled injected wake; no Porcupine account/model is configured. ConversationInput preserves incoming PCM while VAD onset interrupts output. Application --endpoint-ms exposes alternate silence profiles for controlled comparisons.
- session.py implements the lifecycle, explicit exit, inactivity tick, eight-chunk playback queue, cancellation, stale-result rejection and completed-segment delivery history. A future device sink must implement actual stop/flush; the current sink is memory-only.
- harness.py and cli.py provide the Pipecat endpointed-utterance bridge, mock follow-up demo, file VAD replay and optional mock conversation through our speech servers. This is finite replay, not an always-running device service; the future runtime must schedule inactivity ticks and supply echo-controlled capture.
- tools.py provides a bounded in-memory ledger and typed mock task executor now used by Session. Completed effects survive speech cancellation and deduplicate by session/turn/call identity; corrections get new identities. This is not a deployed general task server, physical verification or restart-safe guarantee.

No real-speaker recordings were supplied. The maintained fixture script uses the host's existing espeak to generate synthetic speech under var/recordings/. This is local VAD/transport input only, not wake-reliability or ASR-quality evidence. Detailed contracts and remaining streaming design gates are in ARCHITECTURE.md.

This initial 2026-10-21 record is historical; current M1 verification follows it below. Its source manifest and selected evidence retain their original fingerprints. Do not overwrite them with the new implementation's manifest.

Run from the ME3 root. Downloads and local-IPC commands required approved escalation in this Codex environment. All outputs below remain under ignored var/.

Setup and lock:

~~~bash
python3 -m venv var/cache/venv
var/cache/venv/bin/python -m pip install --cache-dir var/cache/pip uv
var/cache/venv/bin/uv lock
env UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=var/cache/venv UV_PYTHON_DOWNLOADS=never var/cache/venv/bin/uv sync --locked --extra dev
var/cache/venv/bin/uv lock --check --offline
var/cache/venv/bin/uv pip check --python var/cache/venv/bin/python
env UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=var/cache/repro UV_PYTHON_DOWNLOADS=never var/cache/venv/bin/uv sync --locked --extra dev --offline
~~~

Results: uv installed as 0.13.4; the final lock resolves 77 packages across markers/extras, with 71 installed by sync. Lock check passed; all 73 packages found by pip check (including bootstrap tools) were compatible. Offline clean installation succeeded. README pins the observed uv version for reproduction.

Focused regression and clean-install checks:


2. Install/resolve the lock against actual Pi Python/aarch64 in a separate ME3 environment. Measure startup, CPU/RSS, local VAD and per-chunk MCP behavior before selecting production transport.
3. Supply provider account/model/voice access and explicit spending limits before enabling live transport or selecting the LLM. Test authentication, errors, deadlines and cancellation through our servers. Do not implicitly retry paid/effectful operations.
4. After inventory, implement device capture/playback and schedule inactivity ticks. Verify stop/flush, stable devices, pre-roll and echo control using playback reference or verified hardware. Select/configure the wake engine; measure real speakers, misses and false accepts.
5. Validate follow-ups and corrections with actual mic/speaker playback. Then collect BENCHMARK.md acoustic trials (at least 20/scenario, retaining failures). Do not infer acoustic full-duplex behavior from mocks.
6. Establish branch ownership and a reviewed ME3 source base/manifest before later patch exchange or requested staging/commits. Missing specification text and instructor acceptance of any future auxiliary audio channel remain open requirements.

Further milestone exits need access, material provider decisions or the Pi. No deployment archive, boot service, public repository or remote endpoint was created.

## M1 implementation and verification, 2026-10-27

M1 uses production-oriented candidates rather than unverified universal "SOTA" claims: reference-based WebRTC/PipeWire AEC on actual Pi audio; conservative stateful preprocessing; pretrained openWakeWord with Porcupine comparison if needed; local CPU Silero. Optional neural noise enhancement such as DeepFilterNet remains an A/B candidate after baseline capture/AEC, because enhancement can alter wake cues and adds cost/latency. No denoiser was installed and no AEC was run.

Implemented in place:

- preprocessing.py: explicit PCM16 rate/channel validation, bounded chunk size and sequence-gap rejection; persistent Soxr HQ resampling to 16 kHz; stereo downmix; clipping/peak/RMS/DC diagnostics and exact frame/tail accounting. No automatic gain, noise suppression or echo-cancellation claim.
- wake.py: optional openWakeWord ONNX adapter with explicit model/feature paths, CPU execution, asset hashes/version provenance, and one activation per session with stream-clock cooldown. Final phrase is not selected; Hey Jarvis is only a compatibility-test control, not a silent change from Hey Swift.
- readiness.py: standard-library read-only inventory (no capture/playback), explicit-node review-only PipeWire/WebRTC config generator (never applied), native-rate file replay through preprocessing, actual Silero and optional actual wake inference. Reports label AEC/noise suppression as not run and leave partial model frames explicitly unscored. Output paths cannot overwrite replay input evidence.
- artifacts.py shares the var/ output boundary with the existing CLI. scripts/fetch_wake_assets.py downloads only selected official inference assets into var/cache and stores hashes/URLs; scripts/make_speech_fixture.py now accepts explicit text/rate/output. tests/test_frontend.py covers resampling continuity, anti-aliasing, clipping, gap rejection, sample preservation, wake policy, AEC config target validation and actual ONNX silence when optional assets are present.

Dependencies: explicit NumPy/Soxr declarations reuse the existing locked runtimes. The optional wake extra pins openwakeword 0.6.0. Its released metadata requires unused TFLite on Linux even in ONNX mode. pyproject.toml explicitly overrides that requirement on Python >=3.12, where those TFLite wheels are unavailable; runtime selects ONNX. This permits actual CPU inference here but is a provisional compatibility exception: uv lock passes, while uv pip check flags the missing upstream TFLite requirement. Do not claim an unmodified upstream dependency check passes. Resolve/recheck this exception against actual Pi Python before M1 exit; use the uv workflow and do not silently install with ignored dependencies. The installed optional backend is a candidate, not proof it is the most reliable wake model for this hardware.

~~~bash
env PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 var/cache/venv/bin/python -B -m me3_voice.readiness aec-config --capture-node alsa_input.usb-inventory-required.mono-fallback --playback-node alsa_output.usb-inventory-required.analog-stereo --output var/results/pipewire-echo-cancel-review.conf
~~~

## Hey Swift and production course review, 2026-10-27

Decision: prioritize evaluation of Sherpa-ONNX open-vocabulary KWS for the agreed Hey Swift phrase. It accepts phrase tokens with unchanged pretrained weights and no account/API key. This extends the previous two-candidate comparison; it does not silently replace the production detector. The English release's bundled README declares Apache License 2.0; upstream model-license clarification and primary documentation are linked in ARCHITECTURE.md. Porcupine custom phrases use transfer learning plus an account/platform-specific file, so remain a conditional fallback. No training was performed.

Changes: optional `kws` extra in the single pyproject/uv.lock pins sherpa-onnx/core 2.0.1 and sentencepiece 0.2.2. Existing source and application CLI are unchanged. The isolated experiment var/experiments/002-hey-swift-keyword-spotting/ holds the download/inference check, keyword file, coexistence check, synthetic WAVs, README and raw reports. Selected files total 5,499,093 bytes; this is asset size, not Pi memory use. CPython 3.13 x86_64 and aarch64 wheels are published; actual Pi OS/Python/ABI and resource compatibility remain untested.

## Opt-in voice-agent transcript display, 2026-10-27

User confirmed seeing the UI and requested future voice-conversation transcripts. Implemented now, without a live model requirement. Existing report transport/UI is reused. A typed display projection is distinct from semantic reasoning history and payload-free diagnostic telemetry. User visibility of the UI alone does not independently establish every Windows native watcher/permission behavior; that platform limitation remains separate.

Implemented:

- transcript.py: current-session projection with stable turn/role IDs; replacing partial user hypotheses, finalized ASR text, numbered assistant drafts, ordered/idempotent segment confirmation, completion/error/interruption and session reset. Late old-session/turn events and partial updates after ASR finalization are ignored. Interrupted/failed assistant replies retain only confirmed segments; never-played drafts become an empty stopped-response marker. Mock/device sink acknowledgment does not establish exact words heard. Whole older turns are pruned at 200 messages/100,000 text characters; Unicode escaped output stays below the dashboard report-file limit.
- TranscriptPublisher: deliberate single-runtime attachment, coalesced async publication of atomic current-state files off the event loop, orderly in-flight-write completion and final flush. Canonical output is var/results/ui-transcript.json. It is replaceable owned display state, not a raw recording/evidence archive or multi-writer/task journal. New sessions clear it; no cross-session archive is added.
- session.py: optional transcript attachment at activation/turn/final ASR/generated segment/sink confirmation/interruption/error/completion/exit. Segment IDs propagate through the existing Playback queue so identical text segments cannot be confused. Existing history, cancellation and mock task effect ownership remain unchanged. CLI demo --transcript opts in; it rejects demo/trace output collisions with the canonical transcript state. Default demo behavior remains no transcript publisher. Streaming ASR partials are supported by the projection contract but not emitted by the current endpointed mock ASR.
- dashboard.py: only the canonical typed file with display_authorized=true is admitted as transcript content. Allowed fields/roles/statuses are validated; old demo history, unrelated transcript files, reasoning/system/tool roles and extra payload fields are excluded. The source is prioritized within the existing bounded result scan. It travels through the existing HTTP/JSONL/SSH/folder snapshots with explicit mode, revision and session identity; neither text nor its source label confers Pi verification.
- Assistant view: user/Swift bubbles, in-place hypothesis/draft updates, confirmed/draft text distinction, interrupted/error markers, session reset and scroll following only near the bottom. Text is escaped rather than rendered as HTML/Markdown. Mock transcripts/playback are labelled; report connectivity still does not activate voice controls. Transcript text is now intentionally present in generated HTML/JSON/local client files when publication is enabled. Diagnostic JSONL remains text-free. README/ARCHITECTURE document the explicit display exception and bounded retention.

Implemented in the one source tree:

- frontend.py: shared diagnostic controller for readiness replay and PCM stdin. Independent configured wake and Silero decisions, chronological frame handling across arbitrary callbacks, wake once/session, follow-up utterances, silence/cap endpoints, inactivity rearm, reported pre-roll ranges and unfinished input. Events/ranges are bounded at 1,000, recent compute samples at 10,000/model; truncation and partial EOF frames stay explicit. No VAD veto on wake, model retraining or threshold tuning.
- readiness.py: same inference path for native-rate mono/stereo PCM16 WAV and bounded raw PCM stdin. monitor publishes an atomic current report roughly once/second while input arrives, plus EOF/stop/error state. Durations bound input samples, not a blocked producer's wall time. No capture driver, overrun metadata or device identity is invented. Explicit audio_origin, host mode, model/keyword hashes, VAD threshold, state/events and CPU-call timing distinguish evidence. Pi-local-inference stays unverified in the UI. Input SHA-256 now explicitly covers consumed original PCM bytes excluding WAV headers; historical whole-file hashes remain unchanged receipts.
- scoring.py and readiness score: exhaustive annotation schema, matching PCM hash/origin, development/qualification split, wake-window matching/misses/false activations, all-negative exposure/rate, VAD frame-midpoint precision/recall, report/label fingerprints. Truncated/incomplete/non-EOF reports and overlapping ranges are rejected. Tests use constructed labels; no real annotation/accuracy baseline is claimed. The annotator must enforce held-out separation and complete ground truth.
- Existing two-view UI: diagnostic session/source/status, recent event offsets, voiced ranges count, CPU p95, explicit synthetic origin and scores only when the report hash matches. Wake/VAD component statuses are independent. It remains read-only; Assistant mic controls are disabled. The test terminal supplies PCM; the existing folder feed carries reports, not microphone audio. - deploy/rpi/README.md is the canonical target test runbook: read-only inventory, same lock and kws-only setup, recorded trials/scoring, optional explicitly approved existing-PipeWire raw capture, UI targeting the actual test host, physical qualification checklist. ## Continuous Pipecat input integration, 2026-10-28

User authorized trying Pipecat now while retaining replaceable boundaries. Implemented in the existing harness.py, not a new application/framework/source tree. PipecatAudioInput runs one PipelineWorker/WorkerRunner across the complete file. A CaptureFrame extends Pipecat InputAudioRawFrame with sequence and a local completion future; StreamingInputProcessor feeds the existing AudioApplication and acknowledges **ingestion, not generated-answer completion**. The adapter serializes feed calls with at most one packet outstanding, validates complete native PCM16/rate/channels/sequence and limits each packet to one second (CLI uses 10 ms). EOF explicitly finishes the existing controller and then sends EndFrame. Exceptions/deadlines/cancellation fence further input, cancel the owned ingestion task, interrupt Session and cancel/join the worker. Caller-side future capture queues/overruns remain a device responsibility.

The first teardown regression exposed that a CancelFrame cannot release a system-frame processor blocked inside ingestion. Added ownership/cancellation of the ingestion task before framework shutdown; the corrected suite passes cancellation and deadline cases. Original failing run is retained in var/logs/pipecat-input-tests.log. No dependency changes were needed. Our session controller remains the sole owner of wake/follow-up/turn/history/task identity and playback interruption. Our MCP services remain in the actual ASR/TTS path. Consumed PCM is not forwarded to another recognizer/planner. The ordered demo bridge remains compatibility coverage; production recorded replay now defaults to Pipecat ingress. Direct controller tests isolate the adapter boundary for later refactoring.

Changed source: src/me3_voice/harness.py, runtime.py, scenarios.py and dashboard.py; tests/test_integration.py adds direct-versus-Pipecat behavioral comparison, partials before EOF, interruption during blocked playback with task correction/no repeat, invalid PCM, ingestion error, caller cancellation and deadline cleanup. ## Documented service adapters, pause-aware policy and bounded UI pass, 2026-10-28

Read AGENTS/README/current plan and inspected configuration, canonical runtime/UI, tests and recent receipts before editing. Initial project configuration contained only the empty backend example; no approved Pi target/access, service credentials or spending authorization was supplied. No live provider or Pi connection was attempted. This run implements documented network adapters and validates their contracts offline, without selecting a final paid/free provider or assuming an HPC API. Previous mock-only/external-unimplemented statements above describe earlier revisions; current behavior is below and in ARCHITECTURE.md.

Implemented changes:

- remote.py: real Deepgram Listen v1 streaming ASR, Deepgram Speak v1 streaming TTS, Groq multipart Whisper file-ASR and chat-completions SSE reasoning adapters. ASR/TTS stay behind **our MCP servers**, selected through configuration/servers.py/speech.py; reasoning is selected by runtime.py. Shared HPC services can reuse a protocol only if their documented contract matches. Unknown protocols fail closed. Native streaming and final-only file recognition are explicitly different profiles; no fabricated partials are emitted for Groq file-ASR.
- LiveTransport: explicit authorization before selected credential lookup/requests; per-instance attempted-request limits, TLS configuration, no HTTP POST redirects/retries or ambient proxy/netrc credential discovery, bounded wire messages/audio/text, safe errors and cleanup. Only selected speech credential variables are forwarded to the appropriate MCP subprocess. Defaults remain allow_live=false/request_limit=0. These counters are **not dollar limits or durable account quotas**. Real access, allowed services/voices/models, an explicit monetary/trial ceiling and account-side controls still require the user. No key, endpoint or provider response body enters UI/trace output.
- Reasoning: streamed text is segmented for TTS; fragmented calls are held until complete/valid, unsupported/truncated/disconnected streams fail without effects. Tool request/result history is reconstructed for the documented chat contract. Only existing in-memory light tools are advertised, preserving completed-effect deduplication/correction. This is not onit/general task integration. No new mock task feature was added.

Bad audio formats, cross-origin requests and non-loopback Host authorities are rejected. Browser playback retains at most eight unacknowledged chunks beyond Session's eight-chunk queue; segment history is confirmed only after browser `onended` acknowledgments. Stop/interrupt clears scheduled audio locally, fences old turns, and frees server resources. Credentials never enter HTML/WS messages.
- `ui/dashboard.html`, `.js`, `.css` reveal Start/Stop/Interrupt only when the voice bridge advertises capability. Report-feed connectivity stays separate from live microphone status. The current runtime's state and transcript can update over the socket; historical reports remain labelled. The DGX3 ASR is final-only, so this backend cannot display partial words while the user is still talking. Static exports retain read-only report behavior. Browser capture requests AEC but does not certify it.
- `session.py` and `transcript.py` distinguish memory-write confirmation from browser playback-callback confirmation. The mock task ledger and turn-key fences remain the sole action owner; no second framework or Pi device adapter was introduced.

## First laptop browser voice trial diagnosis, 2026-10-29

The user ran the live browser bridge through a working private VS Code port forward and then ended the conversation. The first tool turn made two OpenRouter reasoning requests: the tool call and the spoken confirmation. This exhausted the configured **two-request per-process LLM cap**; four later ASR-final turns started reasoning and immediately raised `ProviderError`, consistent with that cap. After five ASR finals, three subsequent ASR turns failed through the MCP client as `ValueError`; the configured five-request ASR cap is the likely cause, but the trace's generic MCP exception does not prove the underlying server reason. There is no evidence of a TTS request after the first turn. The user reported that the first mock lights confirmation was spoken, and that a later “Raspberry Pi” request appeared in the **You** bubble as a raspberry-pie dessert answer with no spoken response. The You bubble is ASR output, not LLM output; this is an answer-shaped ASR result, not proof of correct transcription. The current transcript file had been replaced by later wake sessions, and no raw browser audio was saved, so the exact ASR outputs cannot be reconstructed from this run. Browser-reported AEC on and input level are metadata, not acoustic AEC verification.

For the completed first turn only, measured HPC software boundaries were endpoint-to-browser-packet **4010.7 ms**, last-voiced-frame-to-browser-packet **5052.4 ms**, ASR request **2496.7 ms**, and first TTS chunk **448.2 ms**. The trace cannot measure when audio became audible on the USB speaker, nor did it establish reliable follow-ups or interruption. These are single-turn observations, not latency percentiles.

## ME2-style mock action activity for laptop testing, 2026-10-31

Read-only ME2 review found **19 intents**, not an authoritative ten-item subset, in its current command cheatsheet. This iteration implements ten low-risk ME2-style actions in ME3's existing typed mock executor: light on/off, color, brightness, timer, alarm, create/list reminders, time and weather. The supported values mirror ME2's bounded examples. The service keeps state only in memory; demo timers/alarms never ring, mock weather never fetches a forecast, and time explicitly identifies the HPC clock. The existing legacy mock-light tool remains compatible. No ME2 code, data, model or deployment was imported or changed. Music, call and message effects remain outside this laptop simulation.

The same Session tool path now publishes a bounded, allowlisted task receipt into the canonical conversation transcript: session/turn/call identity, safe title, kind, status, evidence mode, display value and short summary. A running action is distinct from a completed in-memory simulation. A completed receipt survives speech interruption and cannot trigger another execution; an interrupted in-flight action becomes outcome-unknown until an actual result is learned. New sessions clear the projection, and old-session results cannot update it. The browser renders receipts as compact Activity rows next to the conversation, with visibly labelled **Simulated · Mock** results and restrained action icons/colors. The UI does not call tools, drive hardware, schedule jobs, or infer task success from assistant speech. Older transcript reports without task rows remain valid; task rows are independently bounded and validated, and text is escaped before rendering. A future agent tool can use the generic `agent` receipt kind, but no website/repository tool, artifact link, general Onit harness or Pi hardware executor exists yet. A real Pi adapter must be added behind the existing executor boundary after read-only inventory and device qualification; the UI may show Pi verification only with corresponding verified runtime evidence.

The external chat-completions adapter advertises one new typed `run_mock_action` tool in addition to the two legacy mock-light tools; unknown calls and invalid values fail closed. The deterministic MockLLM accepts exact `simulate ...` phrases for CPU-only testing. A live LLM may choose to call the tool, but its quality and service limits are separate. The configured OpenRouter free-only profile still has only two requests per connection, and a tool action normally needs one request to call the tool plus one to phrase the reply. No live API request was made in this milestone.

## Stage latency instrumentation and Diagnostics, 2026-10-31

The existing payload-free Session trace now records submitted PCM sample count at endpoint, ASR stream opening, normal LLM request completion, and normal per-segment TTS stream completion. The summary derives submitted audio duration (including preserved pre-roll), whether input was sent incrementally to the speech boundary, whether any ASR partial was observed, request→first LLM text delta, total LLM request time, request→first decoded TTS PCM, and total TTS render time. It pairs completed TTS spans by segment and leaves interrupted/incomplete spans unavailable. The normalized read-only dashboard exposes these in an expandable Diagnostics Stage details view without transcript/audio payloads or credentials. The Assistant layout and live controls are unchanged.

The proposed token/s and TTS first-byte metrics are **not yet available**: the current client contract does not provide a trustworthy generated-token count or a separate network-byte timestamp. The existing first LLM content delta is not a token count, and first TTS PCM is later than network first byte. VAD speech-onset latency and EOU correctness require an annotated acoustic onset/end; frontend sample offsets alone cannot establish them. Primary UX measurements remain speech-end→first *audible* response, confirmed interruption→acoustic stop, and verified task-effect time. The decision rules, definitions, and error/quality safeguards are in `docs/BENCHMARK.md#stage-metrics-for-tuning`. No latency threshold or architecture replacement is justified by a single mock replay.

## Opt-in Onit draft-task integration and latency review, 2026-10-31

The user requested initial Onit task integration and continued latency checks. Read AGENTS.md, README.md, this plan, the session/provider/task contracts, recent traces, the existing Onit trial, and upstream Onit README/source. The installed editable Onit checkout is `the separately installed Onit checkout` at revision `3d014cfae043130d956ac042de7142516146e96b`, distribution `0.1.5a0` in its separate Python 3.12 environment. Onit's source `chat()` accepts a tool registry and its `process_task()` offers stream/tool callbacks. The current `OnIt` constructor adds default MCP servers and performs discovery during initialization, so this first voice integration uses the tested `chat()` loop directly with an explicit one-tool registry; it neither adopts Onit's broad default tools nor claims Onit MCP discovery has been exercised. Upstream: https://github.com/sibyl-oracles/onit and https://github.com/sibyl-oracles/onit/blob/main/src/onit.py .

Implemented in the one ME3 source tree: `onit_tasks.py` is an optional Session task executor, selected only by `voice_bridge --onit-python ... --onit-max-requests N`; default remains off. It starts a separate, persistent Onit Python worker and prewarms it when the voice Session opens. `onit_worker.py` uses Onit's actual chat/tool loop with only `write_artifact`: at most eight bounded HTML/CSS/JS/Markdown/text/JSON draft files, exclusive create, under an ignored per-operation `var/scratch/onit-tasks/` directory. No shell, GitHub, deployment, account task, GPIO, hardware or Onit default MCP tool is exposed. The existing Swift Session remains the one voice/task owner; its task ledger shields and deduplicates by session/turn/call identity, marks running/reported/unknown correctly, and never treats a reported artifact as Pi-verified. The UI receives a bounded, sanitized task receipt and filename, not raw tool arguments or credentials. An interrupted in-flight worker can finish its confined action but does not replay the call; automatic post-interruption receipt reconciliation remains pending. The worker currently supports only the exact configured free-only OpenRouter chat-completions route, with zero-price routing, no fallback/SDK retries, max 512 output tokens per request and a separately explicit total Onit request budget of 1–8 per browser connection. Each task reserves at most three calls, refunds only worker-confirmed unused calls, and uncertain failures consume the reservation. No live request was made in this milestone; the earlier candidate model's arithmetic error still disqualifies it from a quality claim.

## Bounded TTS segment pipeline and Onit scope review, 2026-10-31

The user asked whether speech playback overlaps further TTS work and whether full Onit integration would fix multi-turn failures. Inspected the canonical Session, MCP speech client, Qwen streaming TTS adapter, Onit worker, and the saved live timing report. Before this change, PCM packets were streamed into the eight-slot playback queue as TTS produced them, so the current segment could play before its full render completed. Session nevertheless waited for each segment's complete synthesis before consuming the next reasoning segment. Session now places at most two pending text segments in a queue and synthesizes them in order on a separate task; reasoning can continue while TTS runs, and browser playback can drain while the next segment is synthesized. Interruption cancels the group, closes the stream and clears playback through the existing path. Final text remains separate from playback confirmation. A focused event test proves next-segment reasoning overlaps a deliberately blocked first TTS segment; the existing interruption test now waits for an actual sink confirmation rather than an empty queue that could precede producer scheduling. No second TTS inference request is started concurrently by this change, and it cannot reduce the first segment's network/model time by itself.

The archived run's first TTS PCM values were **479.5 ms** and **68.3 ms** after their respective TTS starts (p50 **273.9 ms**), and one completed TTS render was **3117.4 ms**. Endpoint→first browser PCM packet was **3823.6 ms**; reasoning request→first text delta was **1120.3 ms** in its one measured sample. The first-audio path still waits for the first punctuation-bounded reasoning segment, then TTS first PCM and browser scheduling. These are software boundaries; the new pipeline has not been measured against a live service or audible laptop output. A controlled fresh trace is needed before claiming any latency improvement. Changing segmentation or endpointing now would need a quality/latency comparison on held-out speech, especially to avoid clipped phrases.

Onit currently runs as an opt-in, prewarmed **confined draft-artifact task worker** called by Swift's existing Session. Its live artifact trial and offline MCP discovery are recorded above. It is not the primary multi-turn voice reasoner, and its worker exposes only the bounded local artifact tool. Enabling Onit's unrestricted shell/account/network tools or Pi hardware actions would exceed the current project boundaries; Onit itself will not solve the archived correction failure if the outer reasoning request allowance is exhausted. The request limit/error-code changes in the preceding milestone, plus a new live trace, are the direct test for that failure. General Onit task capabilities and a suitable authorized task-tool scope remain an integration decision; do not label the current worker “full Onit”.

## Swift Signal Assistant redesign and task receipts, 2026-10-31

Re-read `docs/references/SWIFT_UI_RUNTIME_BRIEF.md` and its companion `docs/references/swift-voice-task-reference.html`. The previous Assistant placed a large microphone-in-circle above the transcript, repeated connected-state text, and gave messages too little room. The reference's useful principle is that voice presence should yield space when conversation starts; its geometry and branding were not copied. The new **Swift Signal** uses seven rounded bars as the voice mark and separates welcome, status, transcript, controls, and task results in one responsive composition.

Implemented in the canonical application:

- `src/me3_voice/ui/dashboard.html` and `dashboard.css`: removed the large microphone orb treatment and duplicate runtime banner. The welcome screen pairs concise copy with a proportionate signal tile and one Start action. On session start, the stage becomes a fixed 72–76 px status row; it stays compact when ended with history. The transcript is the main region, while task results sit in a separate rail on wider displays and stack on narrow screens. Message sizing, task labels, execution receipts, controls, borders, spacing, contrast, and light/dark tokens use the existing stack and palette. Report metadata remains in Diagnostics.
- `src/me3_voice/ui/dashboard.js`: consumes existing captured-input RMS and received-playback PCM RMS to reshape the bars; it does not create an extra microphone stream. If the relevant source is unavailable, the bars stay in their resting shape. Processing uses only a slow state-driven compression/opacity motion, not a fabricated audio signal. Muted, disconnected, interrupted and ended states have distinct labels and still treatments; full-duplex microphone status remains independent from Speaking. Reduced motion and hidden-tab behavior stop animation. The report-feed adapter now preserves the just-ended browser transcript across the immediate snapshot refresh, and task-list updates return to the newest request while preserving transcript scroll behavior.
- `src/me3_voice/onit_tasks.py`, `transcript.py`, and `session.py`: task receipts may carry a validated execution target, absolute path, and verification-level statement from the executor to the typed transcript. `tests/test_onit_tasks.py` and `tests/test_transcript.py` cover the receipt fields. The Assistant shows “Current request”, “Latest result” or “Earlier result · Turn N”; errors and reported/mock outcomes remain visibly distinct. File previews and downloads appear only when the bounded artifact route supplies them. A reported receipt is not relabelled verified success.

## Latest browser voice run and task-widget polish, 2026-10-31

Reviewed `var/results/voice-7cb19bfe9b7a4081b7e397178e976449.json` and its event trace, plus transcript archive `var/results/voice-sessions/e7aa7d74b273446595cf8c7c33392389.json`. The session used external HPC ASR/TTS and the configured free-only OpenRouter reasoning model; the light effect was the in-memory mock. One wake event and six VAD onsets were recorded. Five ASR finals were archived: “turn on the lights”, “Bye-bye.”, “He's dead.”, “Hey Swift”, and “harry swift”. The sixth input ended on inactivity without a final. No raw microphone recording was available, so the text can be reported but its accuracy against the spoken words cannot be checked. No partial ASR text reached the transcript in this run.

Turn 1 invoked one simulated light-on task, then its spoken response was interrupted before any confirmed assistant text was archived. Turn 2 completed “Goodbye! Have a great day.” with browser sink acknowledgment. Turns 3–5 failed before a new reasoning request was sent; each reports `request_limit_reached` with `used=2`, `limit=2`, and `remaining=0`. This is the ME3 per-run reasoning cap, not evidence of an OpenRouter HTTP 429 or a provider daily quota. Turn 6 was incomplete after the recorded inactivity timeout. The action result is explicitly mock and does not establish a physical light change.

### Latency evidence and limits

All values below are monotonic software observations from this one run, with small sample counts. They are not acoustic measurements and should not be treated as stable percentiles:

| Boundary | Count | p50 | p95 | Interpretation |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| ASR request | 5 | 1,846 ms | 2,183 ms | Request span; not a clean isolated model-compute measurement. |
| Endpoint to ASR final | 5 | 150 ms | 173 ms | Endpoint-to-final event interval; not total ASR request time. |
| LLM request to first segment | 2 | 1,300 ms | 1,583 ms | Model/harness text availability boundary. |
| TTS first decoded PCM chunk | 3 | 93 ms | 516 ms | Decoded software PCM availability, not an audible first byte. |
| TTS render total | 2 | 910 ms | 1,110 ms | Full render boundary for completed renders. |
| Endpoint to first browser packet sent | 2 | 1,796 ms | 2,278 ms | Browser transport send, not sound from the speaker. |
| Last voiced frame to first browser packet sent | 2 | 2,821 ms | 3,317 ms | Composite software boundary; no acoustic output timestamp. |
| Last voiced frame to verified mock task | 1 | 2,809 ms | 2,809 ms | Completion in the in-memory mock ledger only. |
| Interrupt request to browser stop message sent | 1 | 1.7 ms | 1.7 ms | Local message dispatch, not microphone-to-speaker acoustic interruption. |

The available sample suggests that ASR request span and time to the first LLM segment deserve attention, while TTS produced its first decoded chunk quickly in two of three observations. These timings have different start/end definitions and must not be added as though they were a single critical-path decomposition. The report has no audible-response, interruption-to-acoustic-stop, tokens/second, or physical-task-completion measurement. Recheck the next runs with a consistent event protocol and a real acoustic loopback before comparing perceived latency.

### Request cap and free alternatives

Raised only the ignored local `var/cache/voice-backends.json` LLM `request_limit` from 2 to 12, retaining `nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning:free`. Configuration validation passed. This is a maximum number of reasoning requests per bridge process, not a spend limit or account quota. The already-ended bridge was not restarted and no model request was made during this review; the next bridge process must load this file for the higher cap to apply.

OpenRouter documents free-variant limits of 20 requests/minute and 50/day for accounts without the qualifying credit purchase; failed attempts count toward the daily total. Its `openrouter/free` route can choose a currently available free model that supports request features such as tool calling. This shares the same OpenRouter account quota and can change the selected model from request to request. It is a candidate for a genuine model/provider availability failure, not a fix for the local two-request cap. Current ME3/OpenRouter and Onit guards accept an explicit `:free` model and reject the `openrouter/free` alias, so that route is not integrated or verified. See [OpenRouter free model routing and limits](https://openrouter.ai/collections/free-models) and [the free router feature selection](https://openrouter.ai/discover).

Google Gemini API is another possible free-tier provider for selected models, but it needs a new API key and a dedicated adapter/contract test. Google says free-tier content may be used to improve its products; its OpenAI compatibility layer has tool-mapping limitations. No Gemini account, key, live call, or adapter is configured. See [Gemini API pricing and free-tier terms](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing), [OpenAI compatibility](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/openai), and [partner integration limitations](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/partner-integration). For the next laptop run, keep the known free-only model and 12-request process cap; if the trace later shows an actual provider rate-limit/unavailable error, add and mock-test a distinct free-router profile before switching the live model.

## Audible wake confirmation, 2026-11-01

Added a short, low-level two-note browser chime on the actual `wake_detected_file` runtime event. It plays once per accepted wake session through the existing browser `AudioContext`, so no extra microphone stream, TTS request, provider quota or runtime state inference is involved. It does not play merely because a status changes to Listening, for injected/mock wake events, or on ordinary follow-up turns. I chose a brief sound instead of saying “I’m listening”: the user may speak the command immediately after “Hey Swift”, and a spoken acknowledgment could mask that first command and worsen speaker echo. If browser audio output is unavailable, the optional cue fails quietly and capture continues.

```bash

PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH=var/cache/playwright PYTHONPATH=src PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 NUMBA_CACHE_DIR=var/cache/numba OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 timeout 180 var/cache/venv/bin/python -B scripts/check_voice_ui.py --output-dir var/results/ui-wake-chime > var/logs/ui-wake-chime.log 2>&1

var/cache/venv/bin/ruff format --check scripts/check_voice_ui.py
PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONPATH=src var/cache/venv/bin/python -B -m me3_voice.dashboard export --output var/results/me3-dashboard.html
```

Results: JavaScript syntax, Ruff lint/format, and static dashboard export passed. The Chromium voice-UI contract passed with mock transport; it verified a listening-status update alone does not make a sound, an accepted wake fixture schedules exactly two tones, and a duplicate event for the same session does not repeat them. The browser check used explicit test events and does not establish that a physical laptop speaker plays the cue at a comfortable level, that the microphone does not capture it, or that acoustic interruption/AEC is reliable. The next live laptop run should confirm the chime is audible but unobtrusive and does not delay or obscure the first spoken command.

## Scoped Onit search and credential setup, 2026-11-01

Inspected the installed Onit checkout read-only and compared its bundled tool documentation with the requested GitHub, Tavily and Hugging Face keys. The installed Onit version uses `OLLAMA_API_KEY` for its own web-search API (with DuckDuckGo fallback), `OPENWEATHERMAP_API_KEY` for its structured `get_weather` tool, `GITHUB_TOKEN` for the broad repository tool, and `HF_TOKEN` for model/dataset downloads. It does not natively consume `TAVILY_API_KEY`. Tavily can search the web for a current weather page and source, but that is search output rather than a structured weather/forecast response. A direct weather-service key has not been provided.

Implemented the following bounded, project-local path:

- `credentials.py` now accepts three explicit ME3 names: `ME3_ONIT_GITHUB_TOKEN`, `ME3_ONIT_TAVILY_API_KEY`, and `ME3_ONIT_HF_TOKEN`. New `onit_setup.py` offers `configure` and `status`. `configure` uses masked terminal prompts, writes only `var/cache/onit-secrets.env` with owner-only permissions, does not print values, refuses overwrites, and makes no network calls. `status` prints presence only. Existing OpenRouter/DGX3 credentials remain in `var/cache/voice-backends.env`; setup neither reads nor modifies global Onit keychain/config or ME2 files.
- `voice_bridge.py` accepts a separate `--onit-secrets-file`; it loads only the keys required by enabled features. `--onit-tavily-credits N` defaults to `0` (disabled); each call uses only Tavily basic search, and the worker reserves no more than the configured credit count over the bridge lifetime. The user selected a one-basic-search-credit ceiling for the first live test. `--onit-github-readonly` is opt-in and exposes repository get/list only, at most three reads per task. These tools are registered in the isolated Onit worker's `ToolRegistry`; no unrestricted default Onit MCP servers, shell or code execution are launched.
- `onit_worker.py` adds a fixed-endpoint Tavily search adapter and a read-only GitHub API adapter. Both bound inputs, result sizes and timeouts, avoid redirects/environment proxies, redact credential/error bodies, and accept injectable client factories for offline contract checks. Tavily uses `search_depth=basic`, `max_results=3`, no raw page content, and returns bounded links/dates. A response without artifacts now has explicit `local-answer` mode instead of being assigned a draft-artifact receipt.
- Hugging Face credentials are stored if entered but are deliberately not passed into this worker: it has no model/dataset download action or shell. GitHub create/fork/delete and broader filesystem/shell/deployment mutations remain unavailable pending the user's requested spoken approval flow. Existing `write_artifact` and the separately authorized one-empty-directory action remain scoped as before.
- README documents masked setup/status commands and the live bridge flags. The outer model tool description reflects whether Tavily search and GitHub read are enabled. The architecture remains provider-swappable but the current Onit executor accepts only the existing free OpenRouter chat contract. Ollama remains a comparison candidate: its cloud tier is token-billed rather than unlimited/free, while local inference avoids per-call API billing but still needs quality/latency evaluation on the Pi 5 with 4 GB. No Ollama credential/model change was made.

## Spotify receiver readiness and persistent authorization, 2026-11-01

The user wants uninterrupted Bruno Mars playback first, then a separate correction/interruption trial to Maroon 5, without repeatedly opening a Spotify tab or manually selecting a song. Official contract review confirms that Web API app/OAuth authorization controls an existing receiver; it does not create an audio player. Recommended target placement is a Spotify desktop client on the laptop now and an authorized Soloist receiver on the Pi later. Swift owns voice/UI task requests, Spotify renders through that receiver to the selected OS speaker. The embedded Web Playback SDK requires browser-side Spotify token access and new DRM/autoplay/CSP integration; it is not implemented or enabled under the existing server-side credential rule. The user asked for a recommendation after that distinction; this pass prepares the receiver approach.

Implemented in `music.py`:

- Read-only device discovery before search, validated device IDs/flags and bounded responses. Select a configured unrestricted receiver, otherwise the sole active unrestricted receiver or the sole available unrestricted receiver. Explicitly target the resulting device ID, including an available inactive device, without a manual play/pause prerequisite. Missing, restricted, ambiguous and absent configured receivers fail before search/mutation. Recheck operation revision after discovery and before mutation; no cached device ID silently reroutes to another speaker. A disappearing receiver may still reject a live request; live activation behavior remains unverified.
- `music inspect --config var/cache/music.json`: lists safe receiver metadata and chosen target/readiness, never starts music, exits nonzero on unavailable/ambiguous/auth state. This avoids spending ASR/LLM/TTS calls before receiver setup is ready.
- New PKCE setup preserves a refresh token and public client ID; `authorize --renew` explicitly replaces existing credentials while preserving device configuration. `credentials.py` allowlists the Spotify refresh token. Credentials remain private in ignored `var/cache/spotify.env`; refresh writes are atomic, owner-only and preserve unrelated keys. Default setup still refuses overwrites. The old access-only store cannot recover a discarded refresh token; one fresh authorization is required.
- Serialized refresh on a definite API 401, retain the prior refresh token when Spotify omits a rotated replacement, and retry only the rejected request once. No retry of uncertain playback effects, timeouts, device errors or rate limits. A post-playback observation cannot retry the completed play. Report playing/paused only when both the returned target device and track match; audible output remains unverified.
- Symbolic music errors now propagate into existing traces. UI recovery wording describes the receiver prerequisite instead of prescribing manual track play/pause. Regenerated the export. Continuous player polling, track progress/volume controls and direct UI playback buttons remain pending; existing voice tools and task receipts are retained.

Prepared `scripts/start_swift_laptop.ps1`: run locally on Windows after installing/logging into Spotify desktop once. It validates a loopback Swift URL, starts the registered native Spotify client if absent, bounds process startup wait, and opens Swift. It does not install software, start a song/microphone, change services or create a tunnel. The HPC bridge cannot launch laptop applications itself. PowerShell is unavailable on this Linux host, so the launcher is prepared/reviewed but not Windows-verified. No laptop/Pi process was started here.

A single authorized **HPC-live read-only** device-list probe with the existing project token was rejected as expired. Safe inspection confirmed the legacy store has neither refresh token nor public client-ID config. Device availability is therefore **unavailable**, not an observed zero-device list. No keys, headers or response bodies were logged; no playback/model request occurred. Sanitized result: `var/results/spotify-receiver-preflight.json`. The actual private files were not overwritten during development.

## Spotify authorization failure feedback and Soloist option, 2026-11-01

The user's `authorize --renew` attempt reached the hidden callback prompt, then `argparse` printed only a generic error. The exact cause cannot be recovered from that output: the prior CLI intentionally collapsed callback validation, token-exchange rejection, network errors, and malformed responses. Updated `music.py` to report the safe failure stage, allowlisted OAuth error code and HTTP status without printing callback URL, one-time authorization code, OAuth response description or credential. This does not alter saved secrets or retry an authorization code. Added a mocked `invalid_grant` regression check.

Reviewed current official Spotify docs. Access tokens expire in one hour; Developer Dashboard refresh tokens expire after six months and their lifetime does not extend on refresh. Therefore the current HPC → Spotify Web API adapter should renew access automatically; it needs another user authorization about every six months or when revoked. The prior ME2-derived token file held access-only state, so it cannot refresh now and requires one fresh consent to upgrade it. Spotify Soloist's API key is only used to start its daemon. Spotify Connect pairing is separate; Soloist stores the resulting session and offers playback/control/state over its local WebSocket. It accepts URIs, not natural-language catalog queries. A possible lower-maintenance Pi design is client-credentials catalog search plus the local Soloist playback service. This combination is proposed and unimplemented; Search's availability under our Developer Mode app has not been tested. Soloist builds also need updating every 90 days. `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` records the distinction and limitations. No Spotify token, refresh request, playback, receiver, laptop process or device was accessed or changed in this turn.

## Confirmed Spotify visibility defect and browser regression, 2026-11-01

Inspected the user's `docs/references/whatisee.PNG`: the voice session is visibly connected and awaiting wake, while the entire Spotify side panel is absent. The earlier repeated environment/restart advice was incorrect. Root cause is in the canonical frontend: `accept(next)` replaces `data` on every report poll/import. `/api/snapshot` has no `live` field. Spotify visibility, connection, and polling all consulted the replaceable `data.live`, so the first two-second report refresh erased the effective live capability, hid the player and caused Start's Spotify connect attempt to return silently. This explains a functioning voice session with no Spotify UI and supersedes the prior stale-page/configuration hypotheses.

Fixed by capturing `const livePage = data.live === true` once from the served page and using that immutable page capability for all Spotify/live-runtime gates. Report polling and imports can update reports without changing runtime capabilities. An imported report with `live=true` cannot enable live operations on an offline export. Canonical build marker is now `swift-studio-5`; regenerated `var/results/me3-dashboard.html`.

Extended the existing `scripts/check_voice_ui.py` runner with `--spotify-only`. It uses virtual loopback page routes and an explicitly mocked Spotify SDK, no real API or audio device. It waits for automatic snapshot replacement BEFORE clicking Start, verifies the visible connected player after multiple further polls, imports a report, ends/restarts the voice session, and checks that only one Spotify player was constructed. It also checks that an offline page stays offline after importing `live=true`. Inspected screenshots at 1280×720 and 390×844; Spotify is visible in the side panel and below conversation respectively, without horizontal overflow. Evidence: `var/results/spotify-refresh-fix/spotify-refresh-checks.json` and `mock-spotify-after-poll-{desktop,narrow}.png`.

## Fragmented OAuth response fix and completed SDK consent, 2026-11-01

The user encountered the generic invalid-authorization-response error, then retried and completed consent successfully. Found a concrete transport parsing defect: four Spotify code paths used one `response.content.read(n)` call as if it returned the entire body. aiohttp may return a network fragment before EOF, leading to JSONDecodeError for a valid segmented token/status response. Replaced these with `read_spotify_body`, which collects through EOF under the existing size bounds. Callback URL parsing now handles surrounding copy/paste whitespace/quotes and reports a callback-stage failure safely; invalid complete token JSON gets a distinct token-exchange-stage message without response contents. The discarded failed attempt's exact response is unavailable, so fragmentation is a verified possible cause, not a retrospective claim about its bytes.

## Runtime reliability, music compatibility and Pi readiness, 2026-11-01

### Latest user observations and evidence quality

Recorded the user's observations separately from the server evidence: the user heard speaker output during testing (audibility in that test only); valid music commands were initially recognized during playback; unwanted extra utterances appeared while Swift remained in Listening; music volume did not appear to lower while the user spoke; and “play maroon file” was intended to mean “play Maroon Five.” Foreign-language recognition and music leakage are suspected, not established. A speaker sound observation does not timestamp first audible output or establish that every playback event was heard.

The latest two-session music trace review above shows bad ASR finals both while Spotify state was reported playing and outside confirmed playback intervals. The saved traces contain no raw synchronized microphone/playback-reference signal and no dedicated playback-only silence interval. Therefore they cannot establish that the music caused those transcripts, whether the microphone AEC cancelled any echo, or whether an ASR language hallucination occurred. The earlier browser flag `browser_aec_reported=true` only reports the track constraint. No acoustic cancellation ratio, synchronized reference alignment, intelligibility score, physical speech onset, or audible interruption stop is available. The recognized “play maroon file” trial was cancelled before an action; a later request was understood as Maroon 5. A narrow query normalization now maps exactly “maroon file” to the Spotify query “Maroon 5” while keeping the original ASR text. It does not modify other uses of “file,” correct the model transcript, or prove better recognition.

### Timeout, tool receipts and recovery

Inspection confirmed that the saved turn with 41.23 s of LLM work ended under a 45 s whole-turn deadline while speech/playback still had work to do. The trace records 2/20 requests; there is no evidence that this error was quota exhaustion. Tool invocation, Spotify state acknowledgement, and TTS/browser packet events were recorded before the timeout. The action had completed once, but the assistant transcript ended blank/error. This is a whole-turn envelope problem layered over a very slow provider response; the available trace does not separate provider queueing/network time from inference because the service provides no server timing headers.

The live bridge now derives an outer deadline from the configured ASR, LLM and TTS per-request deadlines, one bounded music task, the browser flush allowance and overhead. The previous 45 s envelope could overlap a valid per-request response; the default mock-backend calculation is now 290 s. Each provider call remains individually bounded by its configured timeout, and no model request limit or spending budget was raised. Opt-in Onit adds its bounded worker allowance. This prevents premature whole-turn cancellation but does not make a 41 s model response acceptable; the next live run must verify the deadline and provider behavior. The formula budgets the existing two-reasoning-round action path, not every possible eight-round tool loop.

For trusted task results (the existing in-memory simulated actions, Spotify action receipts, and bounded local artifact receipts), Session now speaks a concise confirmation from the receipt and skips an avoidable post-tool LLM call. This reduces one extra model request for those tasks; no comparable live before/after latency sample has been collected. When TTS itself fails, the UI/archived transcript still carries the completed task receipt and stage-specific TTS error, but no spoken fallback can be claimed if the TTS service is unavailable. Failed reasoning before a task has a regression test confirming zero effects and recovery on the next turn. A completed mock task receipt also survives interruption and a later TTS failure without re-executing the action. TranscriptPublisher writes the current snapshot and archives the prior session under `var/results/voice-sessions/` on a clean connection close; a reconnect begins a new active session and the saved archive remains available for import/history. Abrupt process loss can occur before a pending periodic write and is not a durable task journal.

Timeout/parse telemetry now separates request submission, response headers, first SSE event, first tool delta, validated tool call, argument parsing, action execution, post-tool reasoning, TTS and browser send. A provider's internal queue and compute remain combined in request-to-headers without provider timing headers. Errors distinguish `response_parse`, reasoning, tool, TTS, playback and deadline stages; payloads and credentials remain excluded.

### Captured audio, VAD and UI state

The connected path is browser PCM → existing wake detector and Silero VAD → Session input/turn acceptance → ASR MCP → configured reasoning/tool owner → TTS MCP → bounded browser playback queue/acknowledgment. The microphone transport remains active during assistant output by design. Session returns to `LISTENING` after each committed turn so it can receive follow-ups; that label alone does not mean a user utterance is open. `input_open` separately marks an accepted user turn, and `capture_active` reports the active microphone transport. The UI now says “Ready for your next request” when input is not open and reserves “Listening…” for an open user turn. UI browser verification was attempted but the sandbox rejected its loopback test bind; this state synchronization change has source checks but needs a real browser run.

During playback or while Spotify reports playing, the existing VAD path now holds a candidate and requires 5 voiced frames in an 8-frame window (about 160 ms of voiced input within 256 ms) before accepting a barge-in. It preserves pre-roll and the candidate PCM, keeps capture running, and does not require English or reject unusual words. A transient one-frame/music artifact is rejected; sustained music vocals may still pass. This is a bounded false-turn guard, not AEC or speaker recognition, and its software fixture is not evidence of improved acoustic accuracy.

### Action routing and ME2 compatibility matrix

Voice `control_music` and UI music buttons now share `MusicController`; operations carry a unique operation ID and do not re-run on a UI/state change. Real Spotify is used only when the ignored ME3-local configuration explicitly selects it; otherwise behavior remains a labelled simulation. A play receipt reports Spotify/player state, not audibility. The exact ASR phrase “maroon file” is retained in the transcript and normalized only in the downstream search query.

| ME2 command and original behavior | Accepted parameters | ME2 dependency / hardware assumption | ME3 route and configured target | Verification and gap |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `PLAY_MUSIC`, `PAUSE`, `STOP`, `NEXT`, `VOLUME_UP`, `VOLUME_DOWN`: play/resume configured audio, pause/stop, skip next, and change volume by the configured 10% step. | Play may use a configured track/playlist; the other ME2 actions take no slot. | ME2 `MusicService` selects its configured mpv, Spotify Connect/Soloist, or mock backend; audio depends on the configured Pi player/output. | `control_music` → shared `MusicController`; voice requests and Assistant controls use one operation path. All supported device/time/weather/reminder calls use the existing task executor and session transcript; this is an application tool contract, not another MCP server. Tests cover action idempotency, completed receipts surviving speech interruption, schedule replacement/cancellation, reminder persistence, weather failures and UI widget projections. The Pi adapter has not been imported on aarch64 or used with GPIO. ME2 remains read-only and no ME2 tree/config/checkpoint was copied. Calls and messages remain gated until the user supplies an explicit project demo target, the Pi's paired-phone setup is available, and real-call/SMS testing is separately authorized.

### Ducking and AEC trial plan

The user-reported constant music volume matches the actual previous implementation gap: that test predates ducking. The current ignored `var/cache/music.json` was inspected without printing secrets and has `ducking.enabled=false`, so the feature is presently disabled as well. The file selects `web_playback_sdk`, but no live bridge process was inspected, so this config is not evidence of what an already-running process loaded. The opt-in implementation lowers only a configured, currently playing Spotify target after accepted wake/VAD onset, verifies the target's volume feedback, and restores the saved value only if the same device still reports the ducked value. An explicit volume command takes ownership of the new level; a different player or changed value prevents restoring over an external/user change. It never resumes paused/stopped music. Duck and normal controls share a lock. Spotify documents that its Web API volume endpoint targets the current device, requires Premium, and does not guarantee ordering relative to other Player API calls; ME3 serializes its own controls and reads volume back, but external Spotify-app controls can still race the result. [Spotify Set Playback Volume](https://developer.spotify.com/documentation/web-api/reference/set-volume-for-users-playback). These concurrency/restoration rules pass mocks; no volume has been changed in this work. Keep ducking off during the fixed-level AEC baseline.

One combined user-assisted laptop sequence is prepared for the next acoustic run, with fixed wired mic/speaker, position and volume, `ducking.enabled=false`, and explicit user consent before recording: (1) 20–30 s of Spotify playback with the user silent, noting any wake/VAD/ASR event; (2) one known phrase without music as the speech reference; (3) two known phrases during the same playback, including “Hey Swift, play Maroon Five” and a short non-music follow-up. Preserve exact expected words and the bridge trace. If a synchronized mic sample and the same playback reference cannot be acquired through an existing authorized path, record that limitation; browser AEC enabled and unmatched RMS do not substitute. First compare playback-only false turns and speech retention, then turn ducking on for a separate trial. Check Spotify's actual acknowledged volume, explicit user volume override, pause/stop during a turn, restoration, and whether it avoids restoration on a changed device. Repeat only after laptop qualification on the Pi's own output/capture path. No new audio service or second AEC stage is authorized by this plan.

### Latency evidence and current limits

The prior 3.82 s endpoint-to-first-browser-packet trace and the separate latest 42.20 s trace must not be combined. In the 3.82 s sample: endpoint-to-ASR-final was about 193 ms; the ASR request wall clock was about 2.50 s but began before endpoint and overlaps capture; initial tool-selection reasoning was about 2.00 s; action execution was near-instant in that test; post-tool reasoning took about 1.12 s to its first delta; TTS first decoded PCM took about 480 ms; browser send followed almost immediately. In the separate 42.20 s sample: endpoint-to-ASR-final about 191 ms; ASR request wall about 3.07 s (overlapping capture); LLM request about 41.23 s; Spotify action about 0.54 s; TTS first decoded chunk about 235 ms; endpoint-to-browser packet/send about 42.20 s; the turn error followed around the old 45 s boundary. Neither browser packet/send nor sink acknowledgment is an audible-latency measurement. The user-reported speaker audibility is a separate observation with no synchronized timestamp.

After these changes there is **no comparable new HPC-live timing**. Deterministic tests prove that a trusted task receipt can bypass a second reasoning request, not how many milliseconds a live service will save. A fresh live trace within the existing configured request budget is needed to compare the new code. Current diagnostics report stages but cannot split provider/network queueing from inference without service-provided timing headers. Interrupt-to-browser stop dispatch previously measured about 0.52 ms; that is not time-to-acoustic-silence.

## Latest multi-song and time-zone laptop trial, 2026-11-01

Reviewed run `voice-6b6bf2a41c1e4ccb94c08399aff4e202`, its JSONL trace, all five archived voice sessions, current sanitized music configuration fields, and the UI control/event code. This run is HPC-live for inference and reports browser Spotify state; its mock clock action is still simulated. The sessions are separate voice sessions in one bridge run, not one continuous dialogue. No saved microphone waveform or sample-aligned Spotify reference exists.

### What the trace confirms

- Across the run there were 15 ASR finals, 15 LLM request starts, 7 confirmed VAD interruptions, 5 Spotify state observations, 1 manual UI control, and **zero `music_duck` events**.
- In the time-zone session, ASR first finalized only “philippines.” The correction was “No check what I miss it in Japan,” followed by the clearer “no i said what time is it in japan.” The assistant's uncertain response to the earlier wording was interrupted. The clearer Japan question was then interrupted by the next utterance about a song before a response completed. The trace therefore does not show a completed answer to the Japan question.
- The next ASR final was “Stoppit.” Swift invoked the **mock HPC time** tool and spoke its result. This is the task card likely seen under Task details. The recording is unavailable, so whether ASR misheard a request to stop music or the user actually said “Stoppit” cannot be resolved from the trace.
- Later ASR finalized “stop the current song” exactly, but its LLM request failed with `provider_rate_limited` at **15/20** ME3 requests. No music tool call was produced for that turn. The local 20-request cap was not exhausted. A separate “dear song” request received the same provider failure at 14/20. No automatic retry occurred.
- After the voice session ended, one UI pause event was logged as failed; 13.5 ms later the browser SDK reported `paused`. This is a player-state observation after a failed control response, not proof the button caused the state change or that audible sound stopped.
- In a different archived session from the same run, ASR “next song” produced a Spotify task with summary “Spotify connection failed; playback state is uncertain.” About 109 ms later the browser SDK reported `playing` and `track_changed=true`. The trace cannot correlate the state change to the failed API request, so neither success nor no-effect can be claimed. The earlier UI status `failed` was too certain for an ambiguous mutation outcome.
- The current ignored `var/cache/music.json` reports `output_backend=web_playback_sdk` and `ducking.enabled=false`; this run contains no duck attempts. That is consistent with the constant music level the user heard. The configuration file is not proof of what an already-running bridge process loaded. The browser reported AEC enabled and no capture clipping, but without synchronized audio these facts do not verify acoustic echo cancellation or speech/music separation.

### Software changes from this review

`Session` now directly routes only tightly matched explicit stop phrases (for example, “stop the current song” / “please stop the music please”) through the existing `control_music` executor. It skips the LLM request, uses the same operation ledger and receipt, and logs `music_command_routed`. Ambiguous phrases such as “stop it,” “stop speaking,” and the observed “Stoppit” remain on the reasoning path. Spotify's adapter still implements `stop` by pausing because its current contract has no distinct stop operation; the receipt says so. This local route cannot recover audio the ASR transcribed incorrectly.

Spotify transport errors during a playback mutation are now classified as `unknown` when the request may have reached the player. Definite rejections remain `failed`; no request is retried. The task card's recovery text tells the user to check current player state before retrying. This prevents a later, uncorrelated SDK observation from being misreported as a confirmed result. It does not retrospectively determine what happened in the reviewed run.

Automatic ducking remains disabled. The feature is opt-in and no volume was changed during this review; enablement and actual level feedback require a separate controlled laptop trial after the fixed-volume AEC baseline. No claim is made that current voice detection distinguishes the user's speech from sustained music vocals.

## ME2 action coverage and laptop AEC probe integration, 2026-11-01

Completed the HPC-testable portion of the requested ME2 non-music action work. Before implementation, ME2's relevant action handlers, configuration and wiring were inspected read-only; the compatibility matrix above records the original behavior, ME3 mapping, evidence and gaps. Implemented actions use the existing `Session` task executor, not a second tool owner. A single `DeviceActions` service serializes the RGB LED and TM1637 display, deduplicates repeated call IDs, owns timer/alarm schedule state, arbitrates the three-second temperature display overlay, and updates the same structured task receipt consumed by transcript and UI widgets. Time, optional configured weather, and reminders use that same task route. Call and message remain deliberately unavailable until ME3 has an explicitly configured demo recipient/paired phone and separate authorization; no concrete ME2 recipient or credential was copied.

The default device configuration and tests are mock-only. The Pi adapter is prepared for the documented ME2 BCM wiring (RGB 17/27/22; TM1637 CLK/DIO 23/24), but has not been imported or exercised on a Pi. A Pi-mode result means the configured output command was accepted; without readback it is not proof of a physical LED/display effect. Timer/alarm currently have no buzzer or completion speech. Weather defaults to unavailable. Temperature is a displayed setpoint, not a measurement or HVAC command. These constraints appear in the UI and compatibility table.

The laptop AEC probe was connected to the existing live bridge and local dashboard as `/audio-probe`; the live Diagnostics → Audio link opens it. It requests one browser microphone only after an explicit Start action, plays a local user-selected audio reference, and downloads a local WebM plus settings/phase JSON without uploading them. This allows one-repeatable-file AEC-requested-off/on comparison through the laptop browser, with playback-only silence, speech-over-playback and speech-after-playback phases. The JSON records the browser's reported AEC setting, which may differ from the requested setting. Its browser timestamps do not align mic samples to the playback reference, so it cannot produce ERLE or prove cancellation. It tests a selected audio file through the laptop speaker; it does not capture the current Spotify stream or Swift's actual TTS. A separate live conversation with Spotify off is needed to test self-capture during Swift speech. The browser voice bridge continues to request AEC as an ideal-enabled constraint; the probe does not add a production live-session AEC toggle.

The latest multi-song/Japan trace was also reviewed. It confirms 15 ASR finals, 7 interruption requests, 5 Spotify state observations and no `music_duck` event. The clear Japan question was interrupted before a completed response. The transcript “Stoppit” invoked the mock HPC clock tool; without raw microphone audio, it is unknown whether this was an ASR error for a stop command. The later exact “stop the current song” transcript failed at the LLM provider with `provider_rate_limited` at ME3 request count 15/20, before a Spotify tool call. A separate “dear song” request rate-limited at 14/20. This is provider-side throttling, not exhaustion of ME3's local request cap. The current bridge process must be stopped and restarted to load the direct exact-phrase stop route added in source; that route skips reasoning for narrowly matched stop wording and then uses the existing idempotent music action path. Spotify's separate stop semantics map to pause. The current ignored `var/cache/music.json` has `ducking.enabled=false`, consistent with no duck event and the user's constant-volume observation. These logs do not prove speaker leakage: no synchronized microphone sample and player-reference recording was available. Bad transcripts occurred around playback and in other intervals, so AEC, ASR and turn acceptance remain separate hypotheses to test.

### Qwen tool-path diagnosis and integration correction, 2026-11-01

The prior laptop trace did not show a quota response or rejected Spotify command: it contained five finalized ASR turns, each followed by a new accepted VAD onset and cancellation before any LLM response/tool delta. This explains why that specific run had no Spotify action. Earlier, the OpenRouter laptop route did reach `control_music`; Spotify then reported that an active device was needed. A later trial selected a Bruno Mars track and received Spotify state feedback, but audibility remained unverified. Those runs establish that the separate Spotify/action path has worked; they do not prove Spotify was reached by the new DGX run.

Compared actual DGX requests in `var/experiments/010-dgx-qwen-tool-contract/`. The no-tools endpoint remained responsive. The full ME3 tool body and long production `control_music` description stalled before response headers; shortening only that production description made the same inert one-tool schema return headers in 10 ms, first SSE at 1.62 s and a valid function delta by 2.30 s. Several complete production multi-tool requests still timed out, while the concise task-specific single-tool request succeeded. The supported cause is the request-shape/tool-selection path presented to this vLLM Qwen deployment, not a whole-service outage. We cannot attribute the delay to server queue versus prompt processing because server-side timings are unavailable. A separate protocol mismatch was also confirmed: Qwen emitted a complete valid tool call with `finish_reason=stop`, which ME3 previously rejected because it required `tool_calls` whenever calls were present.

Changes in the canonical runtime:

- `ChatReasoning` now sends one intent-scoped schema for explicit music, supported device, or enabled Onit requests; ordinary questions use no tools. Mixed-domain requests do not receive a tool. Music follow-ups retain music focus from prior completed music history.
- A task request uses a concise task-specific system message and forces the single selected function. Ordinary questions retain the concise assistant prompt and receipt-truthfulness guidance.
- Once a task receipt is in history for the current user turn, the follow-up reasoning request has no tools, so it can compose a spoken confirmation without repeating the completed action. Tool output must match a function advertised on that request.
- Tool descriptions are concise. The live bridge uses the typed shared task executor, not legacy direct mock-light functions. `finish_reason=stop` is accepted with a complete, validated tool call; truncated output remains rejected.
- The local model request count remains unbounded as explicitly configured; operational timeouts, cancellation and serialized concurrency remain.

Live, no-side-effect validation after these changes:

- Reproducible `probe_music_tool.py` used the actual ME3 `ChatReasoning` adapter and returned `control_music(action=play, query="Bruno Mars")`, with no task executor or Spotify request. Latest sample: response headers at 11.1 ms, first SSE at 81.9 ms, first tool delta at 4,479.2 ms, validated tool call at 4,945.9 ms. An earlier same-adapter sample completed the decoded tool call in 3.79 s. Variation across these two samples is visible; this is not a latency distribution.
- A separate actual DGX request for “Set the light to blue” decoded `run_device_action(action=set_color, value=blue)` at 1,189 ms: response headers at 10 ms, first SSE at 153 ms, tool delta at 738 ms. It was not executed against even the mock service.
- The isolated long-description production schema produced no headers in 22 s; this and other exploratory timeouts are recorded under `var/results/`. The empty/no-tools baseline previously completed in 0.33–0.78 s. Do not compare these as a statistical benchmark.
