### Active voice session lifetime and barge-in, 2026-11-01

The latest “Concise.” turn remained in `thinking` for 45.0 seconds before `turn_deadline_exceeded`. Inspection found three overlapping limits: `ChatReasoning`'s HTTP/SSE transport imposed a 45-second total timeout, `Session.reasoning()` wrapped each model-stream read in the same 45-second timeout, and the live bridge also passed a finite whole-turn deadline. When that failed turn returned to `LISTENING`, `last_activity` still reflected the earlier input, so the separate 10.016-second inactivity check ended the wake session almost immediately. The model request count was unlimited (`request_limit: null`); this was application timeout policy, not quota.

Changed the live voice path so an active response has no arbitrary total/idle LLM response deadline and no whole-turn wall-clock deadline. The LLM HTTP connection-establishment timeout remains configured (currently 45 seconds); after the connection is established, an active SSE response may continue until completion, transport failure, explicit End, or a new accepted speech turn. New speech still fences and cancels obsolete generation immediately. `Session.tick()` only ends an inactive `LISTENING` session, never active `THINKING`, `SPEAKING`, or open-input work. The inactivity window in the live bridge and recorded replay is now 60 seconds. When a provider failure does return to listening, the inactivity clock now starts at recovery, giving the user a fresh follow-up window. Existing ASR/TTS MCP operation deadlines remain configured independently at 60 seconds.

This intentionally favors an available, interruptible session over silently abandoning a slow in-progress LLM request. A service that remains connected but never emits output can leave the UI in `Thinking` until the user interrupts or ends the conversation; server-side cancellation is not guaranteed by the provider. A network connect failure, explicit transport error, or user interruption still releases the local response stream. No physical mic, audible interruption or Pi behavior was verified.

### Bridge recovery, repeated interruption and current evidence audit, 2026-11-01

Extended the existing reliability implementation without adding a second test runner or runtime session owner.

- `voice_bridge.py` now exposes a same-origin loopback-only `GET /api/health`. Its response distinguishes process reachability, the single WebSocket session slot, lazy versus initialized speech MCP services, and the absence of session resume. It intentionally does **not** claim microphone availability, wake-model readiness, provider health, Pi connection or audible playback. `--host` is limited to `127.0.0.1`/`localhost`; port is explicitly configurable with `--port`, and the default host can be selected through `ME3_VOICE_HOST`. Startup errors for occupied/protected ports give recovery guidance without killing listeners.
- The browser preflights bridge health before requesting microphone permission; permission/device/format errors are distinct from unreachable bridge, wrong server, WebSocket failure and voice-runtime startup timeout. Unexpected disconnect releases browser-owned resources, preserves the runtime error through report refresh, and performs bounded health-only retries. If the bridge returns, the browser asks for a deliberate new session. It does not reconnect the WebSocket, restore a session, or replay a turn/action because the server has no resume contract. A refreshed page can briefly see the prior active slot until the old socket is cleaned up; retry Start after that slot clears.
- Added a repeated action/interruption/correction regression: eight cycles complete a simulated lamp action, interrupt while its spoken reply is blocked, preserve its receipt/effect, complete an unrelated color action and then correct only the lamp. It asserts 24 unique receipts/effects, no duplicate or stale assistant reply, correct final state, empty playback queues and no remaining ME3 tasks. Existing stress and lifecycle tests continue to cover four concurrent sessions, stale-turn fences, reasoning/synthesis interruption, timeouts, disconnect, provider failures and recovery.
- The existing 100-turn test's scope is confirmed: deterministic ASR text injection into four independent `Session` instances, 25 sequential turns each, mixing general follow-ups with simulated light on/off, plus effect-count/history/session-state/queue/task-leak/timing assertions. It did not previously repeat interruption or reconnects; the new eight-cycle test addresses repeated interruption and correction. It still does not perform 100 interrupted turns, audio-to-ASR synthesis, Onit concurrency, or Pi/device stress. The separate bridge test checks one active WebSocket, rejects a duplicate with 409, observes disconnect and permits a fresh socket. A local occupied-port test confirms the existing listener stays open and reports inspect/change-port guidance.
- Current task/transcript contracts already use correlated session/turn/call IDs, `running` and terminal task states, receipts, stale transcript revision/run/session checks, and contextual widgets for Spotify/music, lights, display setpoint, timers/alarms, time, weather, reminders and bounded agent artifacts. Status/evidence distinguishes simulated, accepted/reported, completed, failed, unknown, unavailable, replaced and cancelled. There is no truthful queued/progress/awaiting-approval event source today; Onit runs as one bounded task call and does not expose intermediate step callbacks to Swift, so the UI does not invent percentages or approval gates. Current widgets are event/report projections, not proof of physical execution. Refreshing rehydrates published transcript snapshots; live-session resume/action replay is deliberately unsupported.
- Timing instrumentation already separates ASR request/final, LLM request/headers/first SSE/tool parse/tool call, Onit worker/model/TTFT where emitted, tool duration, post-tool reasoning, TTS start/first PCM/complete render, sink-send start, and software stop dispatch. These spans correlate with monotonic run/session/turn/segment identifiers and aggregation does not sum overlapping streaming stages. Queue wait before provider submission is not isolated for the browser path, and older saved reports lack the Onit-specific worker/model fields; no live calls were made to fill that gap.

### Outcome-first conversation evaluation, 2026-11-02

Fixed the evaluation cases and a minimum useful change before measuring: ten maintained mock scenarios (including wake/command, 800 ms natural pause, slow/disconnected services, follow-up, interruptions during reasoning/TTS, completed-task correction, failure, and 100 turns across four sessions), plus the existing music/ME2/session tests. Any faster endpoint must save at least 150 ms, preserve the 800 ms pause as one utterance, and introduce no duplicate action, stale reply, stuck turn or material p95 regression. Configuration review found DGX Qwen2-Audio final-only ASR, streaming Qwen3-TTS, streaming Qwen3.8-27B reasoning, persistent HTTP clients, Onit `max_tokens=512` and `max_context_tokens=16384`, and provider-enforced request limits (`null`). No live model comparison was run because this evaluation had no explicit per-trial request/spend cap. Exact fixed cases, commands and caveats: `var/experiments/015-conversation-latency/README.md`.

Metric choices follow [LiveKit's session spans and E2E definition](https://docs.livekit.io/reference/agents/session-traces/), its [pipeline trade-offs](https://docs.livekit.io/agents/models/pipelines/), [ElevenLabs agent success/error/latency grouping](https://elevenlabs.io/docs/eleven-agents/dashboard), [Google's concise self-repair guidance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dialogflow/cx/docs/concept/voice-agent-design), and [ElevenLabs' warning that provider TTS latency excludes network and player buffering](https://elevenlabs.io/docs/eleven-api/concepts/latency-methodology). Under-one-second audible response is an aspiration for simple turns, not a measured ME3 result or SLA. ### Opt-in exact-clock responsiveness and endpoint timing, 2026-11-02

Inspected the current path after experiment 015. The provider transport already keeps an aiohttp session across turns; ChatReasoning emits complete sentence segments as streamed SSE text arrives, and Session overlaps bounded TTS generation/playback with later reasoning. Typed completed task receipts already avoid a second model narration request. Those paths were retained. The selected new factor is an opt-in exact final-transcript clock request: `Session.direct_clock_enabled`, `--direct-clock` on replay and the loopback bridge, and a strict `get_time` classifier. It uses the existing typed task, receipt, response stream and cancellation fence. The bridge default remains **off** until final ASR recognition is qualified; requests with a place, multiple clauses, trailing correction or incomplete wording stay on the general agent. Time is explicitly reported as the host's system clock, not a verified Pi clock or requested remote timezone. This is a read-only task and has no physical effect. Existing direct music stop remains; no wider music/light/timer fast router was added without ASR certainty and matched task-accuracy evidence.

Added `last_voiced_frame_to_endpoint_ms` as a correlated same-run/session/turn/clock software timing pair. Reprocessing the latest preserved browser JSONL produced **n=7, p50 1,017.6 ms, p95 1,041.5 ms**; this supports that the configured 1,024 ms silence policy is a real local wait in that run. It is not an acoustic last-speech timestamp. The same trace has endpoint-to-ASR-final p50 199 ms (n=6), reasoning request-to-first-delta p50 2,414 ms (n=2), TTS-first-chunk p50 65 ms (n=4), and endpoint-to-browser-send p50 2,853 ms (n=2). The 7,987 ms ASR request includes 7,904 ms input audio. Small samples and overlapping spans prevent a current-provider latency ranking. Local queue/setup and browser playback buffer are still not isolated by the saved traces; browser send start is not audible onset.

| Outcome-first gate | Before | Retained opt-in route | Evidence/limit |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Five paired `get_time` turns, endpoint to first memory sink | 200.909 ms p50 | 0.333 ms p50 | Deterministic 200 ms model delay, run 1; no real-model claim |
| Second five-pair repeat | 200.992 ms p50 | 0.327 ms p50 | Same fixed cases, reversed order on alternating pairs |
| Final-code five-pair repeat | 200.986 ms p50 | 0.308 ms p50 | Same controlled mock; 5 model calls before, 0 after; one typed receipt each |
| Correctness/fencing | 80/80 focused session/music/telemetry/reliability tests, 34/34 MCP/Pipecat/Onit integration tests | No duplicate completed effect or stale accepted reply in checked cases; ambiguity classifier and direct-route interruption covered | Mock and synthetic HPC software, no physical action |
| First audible audio / actual stop / speaker leakage | Unavailable | Unavailable | Laptop acoustic and Pi gates remain |
| New live request cost | 0 | 0 | No authorized per-trial comparison allowance |

The 640 ms global endpoint candidate remains rejected because it split the fixed 800 ms pause. The live bridge stays at 1,024 ms. A generated synthetic-WAV replay with a scripted mock ASR final and actual CPU/Pipecat ingress completed one `get_time` task and truthful receipt under `var/results/clock-route-replay-20261102.json[.jsonl]`; it cannot establish recognition of the generated words. The remaining dominant wait for simple general questions appears to be remote reasoning startup, but n=2 current browser turns do not prove consistency. A simple exact clock query can bypass that request only when `--direct-clock` is selected. Long tasks continue to have truthful `running` and terminal receipts; the Onit worker does not publish verified intermediate progress events, so filler speech and invented percentages were not added.

### Background task lifecycle, acceptance latency and multi-turn UI, 2026-11-02

Reviewed the current Session/task/transcript path, the served dashboard and experiment 015 before editing. Session previously awaited the task executor before it could acknowledge the action; the task receipt was coupled to the speech turn, and a running task could become `unknown` when that reply was interrupted. The task panel also showed saved active work with present-tense labels and updated ages, while task ordering reversed a recency sort.

Implemented a small opt-in `execute_background()` contract at the existing Session task boundary. Session records one stable task ID, gives one honest acceptance acknowledgement (“I’ve started that task. It may take a few minutes; you can keep talking while it runs.”), and routes explicit task phase/step, heartbeat, and terminal updates back to the originating receipt. Heartbeats do not modify the progress timestamp or phase. Speech interruption clears the spoken reply but does not cancel or mark the background task unknown. Explicit worker cancellation remains a separate action. Executors that do not implement this optional contract keep their previous synchronous semantics.

`MockBackgroundTaskExecutor` and the existing text-injected scenario path now cover: turn on lights → mock Taylor Swift playback → start a bounded project/file task → pause music → set light color blue → ask task status → interrupt Swift’s status reply → receive the finished receipt. The task output is only `project-plan.md` inside the designated `var/results/016-background-task-ui/.../task-output/` directory. Duplicate submission of the same operation returns the original task ID and leaves worker/effect count at one. Separate `Session` mock scenarios exercise failure before output and explicit task cancellation. No unrestricted filesystem worker, arbitrary project creation, real music, lights or provider is used.

The Assistant view now labels saved status as **Task at snapshot**, distinguishes “Recorded · was running · Mock” from live work, freezes elapsed/progress/heartbeat ages at the snapshot time, lists completed steps and heartbeat separately, and sorts receipts by most recent task update. The latest-completed task now says “Completed most recently · Turn N” even if newer unrelated commands were issued after task start. Narrow failure screenshots include a scrolled capture confirming the full recovery message can be read above the sticky voice dock. Two active task cards keep distinct IDs. Browser refresh restores only the published transcript snapshot; it does not reconnect/resume a worker or replay an action.

#### Responsiveness candidate and evidence

Before changing the response path, set the acceptance gate to five alternated matched trials per path with the same fixed 200 ms mock worker delay: retain the async-acceptance candidate only if tool-selection to first mock-sink chunk improves by at least 100 ms, all trials have one worker effect and a stable task ID, and the 120-second lifecycle still ends with one truthful receipt after turns and interruption.

| Timing | Blocking baseline, n=5 | Background acceptance, n=5 | Observed change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Tool selection → first mock memory-sink chunk, p50 (range) | 200.514 ms (200.352–200.815) | 2.808 ms (1.957–5.330) | 197.706 ms mock worker wait removed |
| Endpoint submission → first mock memory-sink chunk, p50 (range) | 200.632 ms (200.465–201.315) | 2.985 ms (2.080–5.467) | Same mock wait bypassed |
| Worker effect count / stable task ID | 1 / yes for all five | 1 / yes for all five | Correctness gate passed |

The candidate exceeds its 100 ms mock-path gate and passed the single 120.045-second run. It improves the path only for a task executor that implements the optional background contract. This is **not** a live Onit/Qwen timing, task-completion speedup, first-audible-response result, or acoustic latency improvement. The paired raw samples are in `var/results/016-background-task-ui/ack-comparison.json`.

The 120.045-second wall-clock mock worker’s correlated task updates occurred at these offsets from its first `running` event:

| Offset | Event |
| ---: | --- |
| 0 s | Running · Planning the requested project files |
| 24 s | Heartbeat only · no phase change |
| 30 s | Drafting the project structure |
| 48 s | Heartbeat only |
| 60 s | Writing setup instructions |
| 72 s | Heartbeat only |
| 90 s | Checking the generated project plan |
| 96 s | Heartbeat only |
| 120 s | Completed · Project plan ready; four named steps and a mock artifact |

The 40.029-second UI fixture confirms the status question was answered from the worker’s then-current named step. Its heartbeat cadence was compressed to 8 seconds; the 120-second run used 24-second heartbeats. The test intentionally interrupted the assistant’s generated status reply before the mock memory sink confirmed any text/audio chunk; it must not be read as a heard response. The task itself remained running, then completed once with its receipt after the interruption. The accepted acknowledgement entered the mock memory sink after 4.211 ms in that run; interruption-to-stop dispatch was 0.125 ms. These single-run mock measurements are not compared to the five-trial controlled timing gate and do not represent speaker silence.

The final served-page check is `var/results/016-background-task-ui/served-ui-final8/background-task-ui-check.json`. Screenshots under the same folder show the accepted, interleaved, interrupted, completed, failed and cancelled states; two simultaneously active task IDs; desktop 1280×720; narrow 390×844; and the narrow scrolled failure recovery. The page was served from the canonical dashboard handler over a temporary `127.0.0.1` listener. It rendered saved mock transcript projections, not a live microphone or task control channel. Its refresh test proves snapshot restoration without UI action replay, not worker persistence through process or bridge loss.

#### Confirmed blockers, not inferred features

- `OnitTaskExecutor` is not an async background task adapter. It creates its worker coroutine internally but `execute()` awaits the worker result, and it rejects a second general Onit task while one is in flight. It has no per-phase event contract. The measured improvement is therefore available to a compatible executor and the mock scenario only; it is not wired into real Onit job execution. The next integration needs a product decision on whether Onit tasks may run concurrently with separate reasoning, and a worker progress/durable task contract. Avoid sending a second model call to query the same busy Onit worker.
- The single spoken acknowledgement is implemented. No delayed 30–45 second spoken status update or proactive completion/failure speech is implemented. The UI has honest phase/heartbeat updates; heartbeat is not progress. A spoken update/completion policy needs an event channel and must wait for assistant/user turn safety to avoid interrupting either.
- Refresh only restores a sanitized report snapshot. There is no live task reconnection or durable resume after bridge/process loss, no browser task cancellation control, and no operation approval/input round trip implemented here.
- Simply scheduling `OnitTaskExecutor.execute()` in the background and returning “accepted” was rejected. The Onit worker remains single-job and a second general Onit call is rejected while it is busy; detaching the first call would make the initial reply look faster but could make a progress question or unrelated general request fail. Production async Onit work needs an explicit concurrency policy, progress-capable worker contract and cancellation/recovery semantics.
- Only deterministic mock task, light, music and speaker sink are covered. No real project directory was created, no Spotify audio/device, Pi GPIO, mic, speaker, AEC, full-duplex behavior or acoustic latency was verified. No real provider call, quota spend or HPC inference occurred. Laptop listening and all Pi 5 acceptance checks remain pending.

Smallest next laptop validation after implementing/deciding the Onit background adapter: one bounded real voice sequence—turn lights on, start a task with a designated safe output directory, pause music while it runs, ask for status, interrupt the answer, and confirm the same task ID completes once in the browser. Capture mic waveform, playback-reference waveform, last speech and first audible response with synchronized monotonic/loopback timestamps; do not interpret the software stop dispatch as sound-stop time. The later Pi 5/4 GB check repeats one light/display mock-to-device command and timer/display arbitration only after read-only hardware/dependency inventory, then separately qualifies speaker capture/AEC. Do not run the laptop task sequence against Onit until an explicit per-trial request/spending allowance and output-target authorization are recorded.

#### Async file publication stall diagnosis and stability pass, 2026-11-02

The earlier unresolved archive test stall is now explained. A faulthandler run of `test_voice_archive_retains_each_session_through_fast_reset` showed the event-loop thread idle in `selectors.select` while the executor worker had returned to its idle queue wait. A minimal delayed `asyncio.to_thread` reproduction also completed its thread function but did not wake the waiting loop on this HPC environment. The behavior reproduced under the project CPython 3.13.9 and system CPython 3.12.3; it was an environment-specific cross-thread wakeup stall, not an archive serialization deadlock. The diagnostic stack is retained at `var/results/016-background-task-ui/archive-test-diagnostic.log`.

Implemented `src/me3_voice/async_utils.py`: bounded file work now runs on a dedicated one-worker executor and its `concurrent.futures.Future` is checked by a 5 ms loop-owned timer. Transcript publication remains off the audio/event-loop thread and stays coalesced/atomic; Onit's already bounded 16 KiB artifact read uses the same pattern. Executors are shut down by their owning publisher/task service. The publisher shutdown test no longer uses `asyncio.to_thread` just to wait for a test event. The dashboard streaming security assertion now inspects report JSON, not the static HTML source, where the Spotify `user-read-private` scope name had caused a false failure.

#### English-only ASR and calmer Qwen speech policy, 2026-11-02

The saved HPC-live transcripts `var/results/voice-sessions/e43631c329b744eaa359e0bbef3147e2.json` and `var/results/voice-sessions/25a49aee0de84a6fa43460d53ecf5742.json` show the foreign-script characters and response-shaped phrases in the **user/ASR transcript**, not evidence that TTS generated those characters. The Qwen2-Audio request prompt explicitly asked for transcription in the audio's “original language”; the cached TTS profile also contained “a brief ad-lib or light laugh is welcome.” Those settings are confirmed prompt-level contributors to the observed failure modes, though the archived data does not identify the acoustic source or prove why the voice laughed.

Implemented a provider-independent user-facing English policy in `src/me3_voice/english.py`. Qwen2-Audio now receives English-only foreground-transcription instructions and a no-clear-English sentinel; it no longer gets asked to preserve the original language. The Qwen adapter and Session reject the sentinel, non-Latin script, and the two response-shaped ASR prefixes previously seen in the archives before sending a turn to reasoning or displaying that text. Foreign-script streaming partials are withheld; an English final can still replace them. Chat reasoning, tool-specific prompts, and the Onit worker now request concise English user-facing replies. Session and Qwen TTS reject non-Latin assistant text before transcript publication or a speech request. These checks preserve Latin text (including accented letters); they are a script guard, not a full language detector, so a foreign-language phrase written entirely in Latin letters can still pass if the model ignores the English-only prompt. The current policy asks users to repeat unclear/non-English speech in English; it does not translate it.

Qwen3-TTS keeps the configured `English` language and `ryan` voice. Its style instructions now default to calm, composed, warm-neutral delivery, with restrained meaning-led warmth/empathy and no ad-libs, laughter, giggling, filler, or sound effects. Required Swift delivery guidance is appended after any custom per-profile style so it remains the final instruction. The existing ignored `var/cache/voice-backends.json` profile was updated only in `tts.instructions`; no secret file was read or changed. No voice swap or sampling change was made: the official model card describes Ryan as dynamic and strongly rhythmic, so timbre could still sound animated; compare a second supported voice only if listening still shows that problem. The same model card documents optional style instructions and English as a supported language; vLLM-Omni documents `language` and `instructions` request fields. Qwen2-Audio's official examples show task behavior is steered with the text instruction accompanying audio. Sources: [Qwen2-Audio official repository](https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen2-Audio), [Qwen3-TTS CustomVoice model card](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-CustomVoice), and [vLLM-Omni speech API](https://docs.vllm.ai/projects/vllm-omni/en/latest/serving/speech_api/). The class DGX3 instance's exact vLLM-Omni version and acceptance of the updated instructions were not probed live.

The dashboard now gives a specific recovery message when English-only ASR or output checks reject a turn. No transcript text or credentials are included in error events. The experiment record is `var/experiments/017-english-voice-policy/README.md`.

#### Confirmed ASR behavior and provider timeout boundary, 2026-11-02

A third direct-route replay was made after wiring provider transport callbacks through ChatReasoning. It used a one-request cap and fixed text injection with the direct Qwen3.8 model. The request timed out 45,048 ms after llm_request_started, before any HTTP response headers arrived (error_boundary=response_headers; one request used of one allowed). The trace has no llm_response_headers_received, first SSE event, text delta, TTS request, or playback output. This establishes the client-side failure boundary: ME3 submitted the request to the configured DGX reasoning endpoint but received no HTTP response headers before its read timeout. The endpoint/model route is correct; the failure is not the local per-run cap, text parser, or TTS. Health/catalog responses do not establish that generation is healthy. Service logs are needed to tell whether the request stalled in queueing, worker startup, or request handling. The approximate request window was 17:38:24–17:39:09 Manila time. Do not describe this as a generated answer or as a TTS failure.

The ASR failure is reproducible without user audio. A synthetic WAV containing the known spoken question “What is the capital of the Philippines?” was sent once through the active Qwen2-Audio adapter. It returned “The capital of the Philippines is ___.” instead of the spoken question (exact match false; adapter time 198.06 ms). This confirms the deployed general audio-language model can answer a spoken question instead of transcribing it, despite the configured transcription-only instruction. The latest laptop “You” bubble was correctly role-tagged ASR output, not an assistant message; the separate LLM timeout explains the absence of an assistant/TTS reply. The laptop recording was not retained, so this synthetic reproduction does not prove the exact acoustic cause of that particular transcript. Qwen's official Qwen2-Audio description includes voice-chat and audio-analysis/direct-response modes: https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen2-Audio . The cached ASR OpenAPI schema exposes /v1/chat/completions but not /v1/audio/transcriptions. The prepared Qwen3-ASR adapter cannot become active until the service owner provides a deployed, authorized dedicated-ASR endpoint and model ID.

The corrected Qwen TTS adapter passed one fresh capped live request: first decoded PCM chunk at 254.72 ms, 599.45 ms total adapter time, and 2.24 seconds / 71,680 bytes of 16 kHz output. The WAV is under var/experiments/018-qwen-provider-routing/outputs/qwen-tts-adapter-smoke-20261102.wav. It was saved to a file, not played or human-listened to. This verifies the current request shape and stream parser, not naturalness, language fidelity of the produced audio, acoustic latency, or browser/Pi playback.

#### ASR task-prompt regression fixed on the existing endpoint, 2026-11-02

The user correctly prioritized repairing ASR independently and will handle Qwen reasoning uptime with the service host. The earlier conclusion that replacing the ASR endpoint was necessary was premature and is superseded by this verified correction. No reasoning endpoint/model, shared service, or deployment was changed.

**Clearly defined fault:** the configured Qwen2-Audio adapter sent the Nov-2 English transcription/sentinel instruction with the audio. The deployed audio-language model responded to a spoken question with an answer despite that instruction. This answer was then correctly tagged as ASR/user text, so it appeared in the You bubble. This is a task-instruction failure before reasoning, not swapped UI speaker roles. Same-audio controlled probes showed that shorter transcription instructions, an explicit system role, examples and alternate audio encoding did not fix it. The official Qwen2-Audio audio-analysis example uses the cue “What does the person say?” (https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen2-Audio#quickstart). That exact cue instead returned the spoken question in a specific quoted “The person says” wrapper. This establishes the observed request-level cause/correction; it does not claim knowledge of the model's internal decision process or a remote deployment change since yesterday.

Implemented in canonical `english.py` / `remote.py`: Qwen-specific official task cue, with English/script checking still applied after recognition; a narrowly anchored parser removes only the complete observed quoted wrapper (optional colon and trailing period). Bare transcription text is retained. Unquoted/unmatched commentary is rejected rather than relabelled as user speech. No broad quote extraction, question-to-answer rewriting, or artist substitutions were added. The existing model ID, service URL, credentials, audio encoding, sample rate and real action paths remain unchanged. The previous turn's MCP error-code preservation and bridge service-specific UI errors remain in place.

Evidence, all under existing experiment 018:
- `outputs/asr-task-fix-comparison.json`: three candidate school-ASR calls. Official cue returned the correct spoken boiling-point question with wrapper; shorter transcription and few-shot candidates answered it. Those candidates were rejected.
- `outputs/asr-official-prompt-qualification.json`: six live synthetic responses. Five matched with the first colon-required parser; the correction case used the same wrapper without a colon. Final actual-adapter parsing accepts precisely both observed forms. Original raw report retained.
- `outputs/asr-official-prompt-normalized.json`: actual updated adapter parsed all six saved live responses with 6/6 spoken-word matches, ignoring case/punctuation. Cases: boiling question, Philippine capital, Maroon Five, Bruno Mars correction, lights on, why ice floats. This is not six independent acoustic or user trials. The boiling question's question mark became a period; words were preserved.
- `outputs/asr-fixed-mcp-session.json` and `.jsonl`: three fresh real-ASR calls through our speech MCP and Session. First utterance was the boiling question; reasoning then failed via a deterministic local injected timeout. A second capital question and a music utterance still produced correct user transcripts. Only the injected LLM error occurred. Reasoning/TTS were mock, output used a memory sink, and no Spotify action was attempted. The live dashboard transcript/history was not overwritten.

Zero edits / 26 reference words (0% WER), 4.971 seconds including setup/transfer. No new capture or speaker output. - Narrow, explicit play requests and contextual music corrections preserve the artist/search words supplied by the user and use the existing music action, avoiding an LLM-generated replacement query for these patterns. - “Can you stop the music?” reaches the explicit stop action. Uncertain Spotify outcomes remain uncertain and are not retried automatically.
- A completed Spotify command is no longer overwritten by a stale, unmatched current-player observation while the requested track is propagating.
- Empty model replies now produce a concise recoverable message. Incomplete reminder requests ask for the missing content; calling/messaging explicitly reports unavailable when no communication executor exists.
- Dashboard task errors distinguish task/action errors from reasoning response parsing failures, and reports with missing or tied timestamps retain newest-first order. No synthetic task receipt is created for a reasoning-only error.

The Groq probes this turn were bounded synthetic text-only probes (26 total requests: six reasoning-mode comparisons, six music-tool selections, eight contextual streamed selections, and six raw contextual selections). Extended the Groq-compatible parser and trace after reviewing experiment 018's retained provider samples. Those samples show the tool-selection model sometimes emitted unrelated music queries (for example, `UNITE`, `play`, and a mixed Celine Dion/Bruno Mars string), while the original user session only saved assistant transcript text and generic `provider_invalid_response` events. The service's free-tier quota/rate window cannot be inferred from this trace. No live provider calls were made during analysis.

Implemented a narrow Spotify recovery in `MusicController`: after a transport/server error on pause/stop, Swift makes one bounded read-only `GET /me/player`. It reports the paused state only when that same targeted player reports `is_playing=false`; if the read fails, the device differs, or playback still reports active, the task stays `unknown` and the UI warns against blind retries. The mutation is never retried. If a later same-turn player observation reports paused, Swift enriches the unknown task summary with that separate evidence but retains `unknown` status and explicitly says causation is unverified. A stale observation from another turn cannot update that receipt. Regression cases cover successful readback, an active player after failure, failed readback, later state evidence, stale-turn fencing, one mutation only, and no reasoning call for the direct stop command.

The time question used Groq because this bridge was launched without the existing `--direct-clock` option. That strict read-only local-time route remains opt-in; use `--direct-clock` in the bridge command to answer exact local/Philippines/Japan time requests without consuming a reasoning request. It does not bypass reasoning for general questions or follow-ups. ASR still needs more examples for “largest city”; this one mistranscription does not justify changing the English model or adding a risky forced phrase substitution.

Expiry uses existing cancellation/stale fencing and frontend reset, returns to the actual Sherpa wake detector, and clears transient pre-roll. Standby retains live browser capture/wake preprocessing but does not submit ordinary speech to ASR or save microphone recordings. Existing published transcripts remain retained. ## False barge-in review and Studio polish, 2026-11-04

### Saved laptop/HPC browser evidence

The user's latest start-only attempt is `var/results/voice-f2df7dba6b7f45e985948a995c07e48f.json`; it contains no spoken turn and its trace records only connection/stop/exit events. The immediately preceding full session is `var/results/voice-sessions/f5dab6274e214e2a81cd3901f68daf3c.json`:

- The two spoken light requests were transcribed and routed. Both task receipts completed once in the **mock device adapter**; the orange update is retained even though its reply was interrupted.
- The snapshot then contains ASR-final turns “Bye”, “I didn't say bye”, “All right”, “I'm going to go”, “Oh”, “Thank you”, and “Oh”. The user reports saying only “I didn't say bye” from that list. This confirms false accepted speech turns in the snapshot, but does not identify the audio source of each one.
- “Bye” is not in the explicit-exit phrase list. The assistant generated “Goodbye! Take care.” in response; the snapshot's ended state does not establish whether the session later ended from the UI or a runtime event.
- No `voice-*.jsonl` event trace matches this full session. Therefore the snapshot cannot prove whether each false turn passed VAD during playback, which browser AEC setting was reported, or which turn first cancelled playback. User-reported TTS leakage is the leading hypothesis, not a trace-confirmed cause. No synchronized mic/playback recording was present.

### Implemented bounded runtime adjustment

The live bridge previously accepted a barge-in with **5 VAD-positive frames in an 8-frame window**. At 32 ms per frame, that is as little as 160 ms of voiced evidence before `begin_input()` cancels the current generation and browser playback. VAD alone cannot distinguish the caller from residual assistant audio. The live policy is now **8 of 12 frames** (at least 256 ms of voiced evidence within a 384 ms window). `ConversationInput` and `AudioApplication` expose the window alongside the threshold so this choice can be changed without altering ASR, conversation or task contracts. Events record the required/observed frame counts, not audio.

The change is meant to reject short bursts while keeping sustained interruption speech and its buffered onset. It may add up to about 96 ms to the earliest confirmation compared with the prior 5-frame threshold. Longer speaker leakage can still pass. This is a conservative VAD gate, **not AEC** and not proof that the false-turn issue is fixed acoustically. The real fix still depends on checking browser AEC state and synchronized capture/playback behavior, then qualifying AEC at the intended speaker volume and geometry.

The session detail dialog now shows the browser-reported echo-cancellation setting (`on`, `off`, or unavailable) and states that it does not measure acoustic cancellation. `getSettings()` reports the selected browser setting; it is not an echo-cancellation quality score. See [MDN echoCancellation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/MediaTrackConstraints/echoCancellation) and [MDN getSettings](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/MediaStreamTrack/getSettings).

### UI refinement

The welcome view now pairs its concise headline with the existing voice focal point instead of centering everything in one tall stack. A small four-bar SVG mark shares the orb's audio language; the “Swift” wordmark and headings use the existing system sans-serif stack. The orb retains its microphone, state-driven processing ring, real mic/playback level response where available, and compact active-session dock. No visualizer library or new frontend dependency was added. Existing state distinctions, controls and conversation layout remain in place.

The visual direction uses the interaction principles in [LiveKit's audio visualizer guidance](https://docs.livekit.io/frontends/agents-ui/audio-visualizer/prebuilt/) and [chat components](https://docs.livekit.io/frontends/agents-ui/chat/): bind visuals to audio/state and keep transcripts and status readable. These were references only; ME3 did not adopt LiveKit's UI stack. ### Evidence reviewed

The transcript evidence is sufficient to identify routing and text errors, but it cannot prove what volume was applied at each moment or explain the latest `What's that?` turn, whose assistant response is empty/interrupted.

The six-turn action snapshot records: light-on and orange as mock simulations; a correct RGB fact; host-clock time reported as `1:45 PM PST`; Spotify accepted `Risk It All` after a Bruno Mars request; and a 20% volume tool task marked failed with the misleading summary `The simulated action could not complete.` The separate `Volume down` snapshot contains a spoken claim that the volume was lowered but **no music task receipt**. Thus that phrase was not proven to reach the Spotify action path. The 20% turn has no assistant receipt and the saved snapshot does not preserve the underlying exception or tool arguments; its exact backend rejection cause is unavailable. The user reports hearing Spotify output and ducking during this trial; these are user-observed laptop effects, not measured volume telemetry or an acoustic benchmark.

The place-name correction's ASR final is exact: `Marilau is spelled as M-A-R-I-L-A-O.` The generated reply changed the final `O` to `U`, so this particular misspelling was introduced after ASR. The earlier Bulacan clarification received `Malilaya is a municipality in Bulacan`, which does not answer the distance question and invents a different place identity. No map/distance service is configured, so an exact route distance remains unsupported. The “PST” label is demonstrably unreliable on this host: `date` reported timezone abbreviation `PST` with UTC offset `+0800`; the numeric offset is authoritative, not the abbreviation.

### Changes made

- Strict music-volume utterances now route directly through the existing `control_music` adapter, without reasoning-model selection. This includes `Volume down`, `Lower the music`, `Can you set the volume to 20%?`, and explicit up/down variants. Unclear wording such as `Turn it down` remains unrouted without music context. Voice and UI volume controls still share `MusicController` and its receipt path.
- An explicit absolute or relative volume change no longer clears a temporary duck snapshot until Spotify accepts the write. A transport/server failure is marked outcome-uncertain; recovery reads player state before restoring, so a possibly applied new user level is not overwritten by the old pre-duck value. Spotify volume failures now receive music-specific recovery wording rather than a simulated-device error.
- The browser Web Playback SDK's initial volume default changed from `0.75` to `0.65` (65%). The user can adjust it in the existing volume control. Spotify documents this SDK setting as a 0–1 player-local default (omitted default is 1); the separate Web API volume field uses 0–100 and returns an acknowledgment rather than acoustic confirmation. This default applies to Swift's browser player, not another Spotify device. [Web Playback SDK reference](https://developer.spotify.com/documentation/web-playback-sdk/reference), [Spotify Set Playback Volume](https://developer.spotify.com/documentation/web-api/reference/set-volume-for-users-playback).
- Explicit letter-by-letter corrections now receive a deterministic acknowledgment that preserves the letters, and the reasoning prompt tells the model not to silently normalize explicit spellings or invent uncertain place identities/distances.
- Host-local clock results now display a numeric offset (for example, `UTC+08:00`) instead of trusting a misleading host abbreviation. Explicit IANA requests still display their requested zone.

## DGX Qwen generation check and bounded Onit static-site output, 2026-11-04

### Endpoint check

The saved ME3 DGX profile `var/cache/voice-backends.json` selects `http://202.92.159.240:8001/v1/chat/completions`, model `Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B`, and the private `ME3_LLM_API_KEY` from `var/cache/dgx3-llm.env`. The Groq alternate profile is separate. The Onit adapter receives its endpoint/model from the selected ME3 profile and currently accepts the exact DGX route on port 8001 (or its separately constrained OpenRouter free route); it does not accept the Groq profile or port 8000.

Fresh authenticated, read-only `GET /v1/models` checks on both `202.92.159.240:8000` and `:8001` returned HTTP 200 and advertised `Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B` (3.5 ms and 6.4 ms respectively). This confirms catalog reachability, not generation health. One bounded generation probe on configured port 8001 used a 32-token ceiling and returned HTTP 200 but no visible text with `finish_reason=length` in 716 ms. A second one-request probe, capped at 192 tokens, returned `4` for `2 plus 2`, `finish_reason=stop`, 31 completion tokens, in 595.5 ms. No key was printed. This establishes that the configured endpoint generated a short response during this check; it does not prove Onit's standalone CLI works from another SSH/laptop environment, sustained availability, voice quality, or a successful website task. Do not reinstall Onit based solely on the earlier CLI timeout; that client path remains a separate diagnosis.

### Website-project support

Extended the existing Onit worker's explicit `--onit-output-root` capability. When configured to the existing parent sandbox, the existing project-directory tool can now create one new named sibling directory and a bounded set of flat static website files in the same idempotent operation. `index.html` is required; up to eight files are accepted, at 16 KiB per file and 64 KiB total, with exclusive creation, no path separators, no overwrites, and restrictive file permissions. The worker verifies the resulting file set before returning a task receipt. Without the output-root flag, website files remain confined drafts in the existing `var/scratch/onit-tasks/` path. With the opt-in root, the Onit model response cap is raised to 2,048 tokens to fit a small static page; it remains 512 otherwise.

Added a distinct `local-project-site` receipt and linked it through Session history and the existing browser artifact preview/download path. The task shows its configured execution target, absolute path, listed files, and a verification label that explicitly says the page was not run, browser-tested, or deployed. HTML is presented as plain text in the dashboard. The spoken receipt also avoids claiming a browser test or deployment. Existing empty-directory and confined draft-artifact paths remain available. No website was actually created in the user's sandbox during this implementation.

The explicit HPC invocation additionally requires:

~~~bash
--onit-output-root $HPC_SANDBOX
~~~

This output scope is opt-in and only permits new sibling folders. It does not grant shell access, package installation, builds, tests, server startup, deployment, repository writes, or modification of existing projects. The prior misrecognized `m8_dash_test` directory remains untouched. Spoken readback/approval for folder names remains a safety gap, so inspect the task receipt and path before using generated output.

## Provider-independent routing, playlist discovery, and delivery policy — 2026-11-04

### Changes implemented

- The existing `Session` → typed task → adapter path now distinguishes specific music requests from discovery requests. Exact artist/track requests still search tracks. “Play a chill song,” “play a workout playlist,” and similar supported mood/genre phrases search playlists. “Play something popular in the Philippines” routes to Spotify playlist search with market `PH` and the query `Top 50 Philippines`; it does not claim that a particular chart ranking was found. An explicit named playlist also uses playlist search. The action is `play_playlist`, and its task kind is retained through the transcript/UI allowlist. Voice requests do not create a second playback path.
- The Spotify adapter searches `type=playlist`, includes the market when supplied, starts the returned playlist context on the owned player, and verifies the resulting player context/device before presenting playback as confirmed. If the provider only acknowledges the request, the receipt remains unverified. Mock mode labels the result simulated and does not play audio.
- This route is intentionally best-effort catalog discovery. Spotify's Search API supports playlist type and market filtering, but with the user's OAuth token the account country takes precedence over the `market=PH` parameter. It also does not expose a dependable playlist popularity/rank guarantee for this use. Spotify has restricted third-party development-mode access to recommendations and some editorial/browse surfaces; its February 2026 migration also removed browse/category and artist top-track endpoints and reduced the search result limit to 10 (ME3 requests 5). Consequently, the app cannot promise an official/current PH Top 50 or a personalized “chill” recommendation. If search returns no playlist or Spotify rejects the request, the result must remain unavailable/failed rather than silently falling through to a similarly named track. References: [Spotify Search API](https://developer.spotify.com/documentation/web-api/reference/search), [2024 API changes](https://developer.spotify.com/blog/2024-11-27-changes-to-the-web-api), [February 2026 Dev Mode migration](https://developer.spotify.com/documentation/web-api/tutorials/february-2026-migration-guide).
- Qwen TTS instructions now request context-sensitive, restrained delivery: calm factual/task responses, warm greetings/empathy, and lightly upbeat positive news. They explicitly prohibit invented laughter, giggles, adlibs, and sound effects. The adapter upgrades the known legacy default at runtime without editing ignored local configuration; custom style preference text is retained before the required delivery policy. This changes generation instructions, not model weights, and has not yet been judged by listening to generated output. References: [Qwen3-TTS CustomVoice model card](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-CustomVoice), [vLLM-Omni speech API](https://docs.vllm.ai/projects/vllm-omni/en/stable/serving/speech_api/).
- Interruption regression coverage now makes the intended semantics explicit: stopping/interruption of Swift's spoken reply does not undo a completed mock music action; without a replacement command the action remains active; a later explicit correction supersedes it with one new action. A long-running mock task continues through interrupted speech and advances on its own phase event; an unrelated light action can complete while that task remains active. Existing stale-search and idempotency tests continue to guard against old track results and duplicate effects.
- A failure-path fix preserves a specific adapter/provider error summary instead of replacing it with a generic simulated-action message. This keeps recovery text truthful for non-simulated Spotify failures.

### Current integration inventory and boundaries

ME3 continues to use Pipecat for browser voice/media transport and session events, with ME3's own session/task router as the canonical action path. Onit is an optional general-purpose task harness; it is not the ASR/TTS MCP server and direct Spotify/music and device actions remain ME3 adapters. The project contains local ASR and TTS MCP services, an optional Onit worker route, Spotify OAuth/player integration, a mock/Pi device adapter, and configured time/weather/reminder task paths. ME2 call/message behavior is not enabled. See the existing compatibility matrix above for the per-action choice and evidence level; this section does not claim new physical coverage.

Onit remains a limitation for truly background execution: its current executor does not expose the background-task interface used by the deterministic mock worker. The invocation is synchronous from the Session caller; its worker operation is shielded from speech cancellation, but the browser cannot receive a reliable completion callback after that call has detached. While an Onit task is active, the executor also does not safely cancel/supersede it with a second general Onit task. The mock multi-minute worker verifies task lifecycle, but does not establish live Onit progress behavior. Do not describe interruption of speech as cancellation of that worker.

## Qwen STT answer-substitution recheck, 2026-11-04

The user clarified that the current regression concerns **STT/ASR**, not TTS. No TTS settings or code were changed during this investigation. The previous assistant launch command selected `var/cache/voice-backends.json`, whose ASR role is `Qwen/Qwen2-Audio-7B-Instruct`; that was the wrong choice for a test meant to avoid the known Qwen answer-substitution mode. The sentence in the newest archived session `var/results/voice-sessions/7c49af0549e84e9fa6d74ca2ca5896c5.json` is stored as a final user ASR message and has no assistant reply/task. Its matching audio and detailed event trace are absent, so the specific live cause is not proven from that file alone.

Ran a bounded three-request synthetic live-ASR check against the existing DGX ASR endpoint, with the current official task cue and one explicit literal-transcription candidate. Output: `var/experiments/018-qwen-provider-routing/outputs/asr-answer-substitution-20261104-rerun.json`; fixtures and reproducible script are in the same experiment's `outputs/` and root. Results:

- The spoken question “What is the first line of treatment for rheumatoid arthritis?” was returned as the treatment answer under both the official cue and the stricter prompt: **8 word edits / 10 spoken words** in each case. Latencies: 374.4 ms and 308.2 ms.
- With the stricter prompt, “Turn on the lights” was returned with an added explanatory wrapper: **8 insertions / 4 spoken words**, 233.1 ms.
- The candidate prompt therefore failed the precondition of verbatim speech capture and is rejected. No source behavior/prompt change is retained; no claim of model accuracy follows from this three-call synthetic sample.

This reproduces the same *class* of failure seen in the user bubble, but not the exact live audio cause: answer-like ASR output is now a strong supported explanation; the missing microphone recording means speaker leakage cannot be ruled out. The UI did not reassign a recorded assistant reply: the archived item is explicitly `role=user`, `delivery=asr_final`.

The official Qwen2-Audio materials describe an audio-language instruction model that can perform both audio analysis and direct text responses to speech instructions ([Qwen2-Audio official repository](https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen2-Audio)). This makes the current chat-completions route inherently less strict than a dedicated transcription contract; more prompt tuning is not a defensible reliability fix. Onit's Qwen3.8 text model is reasoning-only and has no audio input. The Qwen-native candidate is **Qwen3-ASR**, a transcription-specific model with vLLM serving support ([Qwen3-ASR official repository](https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen3-ASR), [vLLM supported models](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/models/supported_models/)). ME3 already implements the documented `vllm-qwen3-asr-v1` adapter for `/v1/audio/transcriptions`, but that model is not the class's currently listed ASR deployment. Next concrete backend step: ask the DGX service owner whether Qwen3-ASR can be hosted on the existing ASR instance and confirm its model ID, endpoint contract and auth behavior. Until then use a dedicated transcription provider for spoken-question trials; the existing Whisper profile also changes reasoning to Groq, so a mixed backend profile is needed if keeping DGX Qwen reasoning. Do not use Qwen2-Audio chat output as an authoritative user transcript for spoken factual questions.

### Research check: common failure mode and suggested correction

This is a documented audio-LLM recognition failure, not a Qwen-only anomaly. Li et al., *A Transcription Prompt-based Efficient Audio Large Language Model for Robust Speech Recognition* (Interspeech 2024), report semantic corrections/substitutions and repeated fragments when a generative audio LLM performs ASR. Their mitigation is architectural: provide text from an expert ASR transcriber and modify decoding; it does not establish that a stronger inference-time instruction fixes the behavior. Qwen2-Audio's technical report explicitly describes both audio analysis and direct responses to spoken instructions. AHa-Bench catalogs semantic/instruction hallucination types in audio LLMs and includes Qwen2-Audio examples. Sources: [Interspeech 2024 paper](https://www.isca-archive.org/interspeech_2024/li24t_interspeech.pdf), [Qwen2-Audio technical report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.10759), [AHa-Bench paper](https://openreview.net/pdf/e9f394ac9fc9947be77b767ff7f1adb37ef7037d.pdf).

What we tried: the official cue “What does the person say?” had passed earlier sampled phrases but failed the latest spoken factual question. A stricter “transcribe verbatim/do not answer” prompt was tested on the same audio and failed identically; on a spoken command it added an explanatory wrapper. Prompt-only mitigation is therefore tested and rejected for this failure. We have not implemented the paper's expert-ASR/transcription-tokenizer architecture or fine-tuned Qwen. The practical application fix is a transcription-specific ASR service/model, with reasoning left to the separate text LLM. ME3 already has a Qwen3-ASR adapter, but that model is not deployed on the class DGX service. Until it is available with a confirmed endpoint contract, use the existing Whisper transcription route for spoken-question tests; a mixed backend profile can retain DGX Qwen reasoning. Do not add semantic “answer-shaped text” filters, since genuine user speech can have the same form.

### Qwen tutorial and Qwen3-ASR candidate check

The linked [`Qwen-Audio/TUTORIAL.md`](https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen-Audio/blob/main/TUTORIAL.md) is for the earlier `Qwen-Audio-Chat`, not the current `Qwen2-Audio-7B-Instruct` deployment. It uses the text cue `Recognize the speech`, but its expected response is descriptive prose wrapping the quoted transcript. I sent that exact cue once to the current Qwen2 vLLM endpoint with the same 3.971-second synthetic spoken question. It returned the medical answer, not the spoken question. Sanitized result: `var/experiments/018-qwen-provider-routing/outputs/qwen-audio-tutorial-recognize-speech-20261104.json`. This is one more failed prompt candidate, not a transcript accuracy estimate.

The supplied [Qwen3-ASR 0.6B/1.7B personal trial](https://note.com/high_u/n/nafc0d70051aa?hl=en) uses the dedicated `qwen-asr` transcription model on CUDA and compares two self-recorded Japanese samples. The 1.7B version fixes some substitutions in one sample and matches 0.6B on the other; it is useful anecdotal evidence for trying a transcription model, not a controlled benchmark or evidence for Pi. Qwen's official Qwen3-ASR repo documents vLLM serving and the OpenAI `/v1/audio/transcriptions` contract. Current vLLM guidance distinguishes Qwen2-Audio as multimodal chat (`/v1/chat/completions`) from dedicated ASR such as Whisper on the transcription route. Sources: [Qwen3-ASR deployment/API](https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen3-ASR), [vLLM audio benchmark guidance](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/docs/benchmarking/cli.md).

The active profile was not changed and no Qwen3-ASR request was sent, because port 8000 currently serves Qwen2-Audio and cannot be presumed to contain the new model. This is the supported route to transcribe instead of reply with a Qwen vLLM model. The service owner must load/advertise Qwen3-ASR-1.7B on the ASR instance (or supply a separate endpoint); after that, run the same fixed speech cases and ensure returned text is literal transcript before selecting this profile. ## Qwen2-Audio ASR format investigation — 2026-11-04

Correction to the preceding recommendation: Qwen2-Audio supports transcription. The current hosted Instruct endpoint failing our cases does not establish that the model family cannot transcribe, that all prompt configurations fail, or that replacing the model is the only fix. Server-side model identity, chat template, processor/version compatibility and audio preprocessing remain unverified. Qwen3-ASR remains an optional candidate, not a proven required replacement.

Inspected Qwen's official ASR evaluation code at https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen2-Audio/blob/main/eval_audio/evaluate_asr.py . Its default checkpoint is the base `Qwen/Qwen2-Audio-7B`, and its input uses audio tokens plus the dataset task prompt rather than the Instruct chat examples. Read only the first bounded row of the official LibriSpeech manifest; its exact prompt is `Detect the language and recognize the speech: <|en|>`. Saved that row's prompt/reference (no dataset download) at `var/experiments/018-qwen-provider-routing/outputs/qwen2-official-asr-eval-first-row.json`.

Ran six additional bounded live requests against the existing university Qwen2-Audio Instruct service, using only the preserved synthetic question/command WAVs. Four format cases compared explicit recognition system instructions, text-before-audio, `input_audio` versus base64 `audio_url`, and the default helpful system prompt. All three question cases returned factual answers; the command returned “turn off the lights” for “Turn on the lights.” Two further cases used the exact official evaluation task cue, audio first and no system message. The question still returned an answer; the English command was described as Chinese and translated as an off command. The latter applies a base-model evaluation cue to an Instruct chat endpoint; it does not reproduce the official base-model inference setup. No production candidate passed, so no runtime request changes were retained.

Commands (first run four requests; second run two; no retries):

```bash

No user audio, reasoning, TTS, actions or Pi effects were invoked. No acoustic claims follow.

Next investigation for the service owner: compare these same fixed WAVs using the advertised Instruct checkpoint's official Transformers audio-analysis example and the deployed vLLM request. ## Qwen2-Audio transcription prefill implemented and qualified — 2026-11-04

This result supersedes the earlier conclusion that replacing the hosted model is required. The existing Qwen2-Audio-7B-Instruct endpoint can transcribe the previously failing spoken question when its assistant response is prefilled with `The person says: '`. No service/model deployment was changed.

Source review: the supplied Hugging Face Qwen2Audio documentation explicitly supports audio-analysis requests with audio plus text and uses `What does the person say?`. ME3 already sent both parts, so merely adding a text prompt was not a missing integration. The supplied tensai GitHub document URL could not be fetched; its published documentation at https://mattn.github.io/tensai/audio/ demonstrates `Transcribe the speech exactly.` with the same Instruct model, implemented in a separate Go engine. That exact instruction still answered our medical question on the hosted vLLM service. The supplied https://arxiv.org/html/2505.20237v1 is a speech-translation/compression study, not an inference-time ASR fix; its Instruct examples confirm audio-plus-text ChatML input. Reviewed documented vLLM assistant continuation parameters at https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/api/vllm/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/protocol/ before using `continue_final_message=true`, `add_generation_prompt=false`.

Controlled results (private university endpoint, no commercial calls):
- Six instruction/reference controls: text-only control preserved the requested marker's words; audio-plus-text marker returned it exactly. Thus text instructions are reaching/followed by the service. The previously passing boiling-point fixture still transcribed correctly inside the supported wrapper. Exact tensai wording and text few-shot examples still answered the medical question.
- IMPORTANT reference correction: the Hugging Face documentation now points to a six-second synthetic `mr_quiller.flac`. Its content is not independently known to be the historical LibriSpeech sentence. The `published_reference` row in `qwen2-instruction-controls-20261104.json` used that historical expectation and its error score must be treated as UNQUALIFIED, not an ASR accuracy failure. The raw file/report are preserved. Downloaded the original Qwen LibriSpeech clip separately; its response retained the spoken sentence with “Quiller” for “Quilter” plus an explanatory wrapper. This also shows that the service is using audio rather than ignoring it universally.
- Three continuation/reference checks: the previously failing medical question and lights command both passed with assistant prefill (zero word edits after punctuation/case normalization); the original public LibriSpeech reference used ordinary prompting and is the separate wrapper/spelling control above.
- Six further synthetic prefill cases passed: boiling point, PH capital, Maroon Five music, Bruno Mars correction, lights on and ice floating. Combined direct prefill result: **8/8 normalized-word matches across 7 unique phrases**, not a reliability estimate. Question/command prefill request times were 86–186 ms in the initial comparison; no audible-latency claim follows and sample sizes do not support a provider latency conclusion.
- Three new actual ASR MCP/session turns passed with the implemented adapter: medical question, boiling point and correction. Reasoning/TTS were mocked, with a first-turn LLM timeout injected. All three user messages retained the spoken words, exactly one error was attributed to the mock LLM, and subsequent turns recovered. No synthetic answer was displayed as the user's question in these checks. Session traces and receipts are saved; no live LLM/TTS or action was invoked.

Implementation: `src/me3_voice/configuration.py` adds a validated `transcription_mode` setting, restricted to Qwen2-Audio ASR when set to `prefill`. The legacy default is `prompt`; current cached Qwen2 profiles select `prefill`. `src/me3_voice/remote.py` uses the proven vLLM assistant-continuation request in that mode, reconstructs the declared prefix when the server returns only continuation text, strips only the completed wrapper, rejects incomplete/truncated output and retains English/error/session contracts. This is structural decoding, not semantic rewriting of an answer into a question. `tests/test_dgx3.py` covers request fields, continuation/echo response parsing, truncated/unclosed output and invalid provider-role selection. Cached `voice-backends.json`, `voice-backends-groq.json`, and `voice-backends-asr-check.json` select prefill only for their Qwen2 ASR role; endpoints, keys and other roles remain the same. Revert with `transcription_mode="prompt"`. Re-running a configuration generator may restore its legacy default; preserve the explicit field when regenerating profiles.

## Latest laptop trial: unintended playlist actions and evidence recovery — 2026-11-04

Reviewed three ended snapshots: `ec1e0b108d0245a0a6a80aecc4e0ee22` (20:22 Manila), `369f0fc3ff284843a2702ae4220131e7` (20:23), and `95d4659a32f045e28affc8b6bb56cf3a` (20:25). The first contains the full question “What is the first line of treatment for R A.” followed by interrupted assistant output; the next two sessions start with only “R A.” The final session includes “I'm sorry.”, explicit Bruno Mars play, “volume level twenty”, “Volume twenty percent”, “music”, “I said stop”, “When I was young”, then “music”. Do not assume the user spoke every stored phrase or that music caused every unintended transcript. The user reports the first interruption was intentional and the later experience was poor; preserve that account separately from inferred acoustic causes.

Confirmed routing failures: bare `music` on turns 6 and 9 reached the model and produced playlist actions, accepted/reported by Spotify as Trending Music PH 2026 and Random Mood. No stop receipt exists in this session. Turn 7's “I said stop” is followed by another user turn without a completed assistant reply; missing detailed events mean its precise cancellation/error point is unknown. Turn 4's “volume level twenty” missed the bounded direct route and its model-selected volume task failed; the explicit percent phrasing on turn 5 obtained a reported receipt. The snapshot does not include raw tool arguments, so the exact bad volume argument is unknown. Full review artifact: `var/experiments/018-qwen-provider-routing/outputs/latest-laptop-trial-review-20261104.json`.

Implemented in `src/me3_voice/session.py`:
- Bare music/song/playlist fragments ask which operation is wanted, without consulting the reasoning model or starting music. Initials-only text such as “R A.” stays visible verbatim and asks for the full request. It is not expanded into an invented question.
- A model-selected play/playlist operation requires affirmative selection intent in the current user request. Unrelated text, pause/stop commands and explicit negation cannot start/change music merely because old music context exists. Rejection occurs before task creation/execution and produces a concise clarification rather than a false task failure.
- “I said stop”/“stop it” route directly to the shared music-stop tool when this session has music-task context; without context, clarify music versus speech. “Stop speaking” is excluded from this music route. Corrections remain new actions, and speech interruption does not repeat earlier completed actions.
- “Volume level twenty” and explicit `volume to` forms now use validated integer percentages on the same direct tool path; the ambiguous bare “volume fifty” remains unguessed. “Play music Bruno Mars” strips only its leading music request word before catalog search.

Found and fixed a concrete evidence-export defect: the frontend emits `voiced_frames`, `window_frames` and `required_voiced_frames`, but the trace validator rejected them. Local-light action events were also rejected because reserved `action` fields had only been allowed for music UI controls. This defect is sufficient to prevent detailed export for such event streams; the exact latest shutdown exception was not retained, so do not claim it was the only teardown issue. `src/me3_voice/telemetry.py` now validates these bounded diagnostic fields and contains an append-only `TraceJournal`. `src/me3_voice/voice_bridge.py` checkpoints the run trace once per second from its control publisher, off the event loop, and flushes on normal/error/cancelled teardown. A lock prevents duplicate appends during overlapping worker-thread flushes. Logging failure does not stop live status publication. No audio/text payloads were added to diagnostic trace fields; existing endpoint audio-sample counts now survive intermediate shutdowns. The report summary remains a final export; checkpointed JSONL can survive without it.

ASR investigation: three fresh capped calls on one generated full “What is the first line of treatment for R A?” recording through the existing Qwen vLLM prefill method returned the full sentence all three times, writing the acronym as `ra`. The strict word scorer reports two edits for `R A` versus `ra`; that formatting difference is not the laptop's loss of the preceding question. Output: `var/experiments/018-qwen-provider-routing/outputs/qwen2-repeat-ra-20261104.json` and its synthetic WAV fixtures. These three calls did not reproduce phrase loss. No new prompt/profile change is justified by this result. The actual laptop microphone audio is absent, so capture truncation, late wake capture, endpointing, provider recognition variability and acoustic leakage remain hypotheses. Do not claim that false interruptions or AEC are fixed, and do not increase thresholds or suppress microphone input globally on the basis of this evidence.

## Guided recording studio and bounded corpus replay — 2026-11-04

Implemented the requested recording webpage to replace repeated ad-hoc laptop voice trials with reusable inputs. Canonical sources: `src/me3_voice/recording_lab.py` (server-owned phrase catalog, private upload routes, standalone loopback launcher and evaluator) and `src/me3_voice/ui/recording_lab.html` (browser capture/review UI). The existing bridge registers the same routes at `/recording-lab`; Diagnostics → Audio links to it through canonical dashboard HTML/JS. The standalone launcher uses existing aiohttp and requires no model keys, wake assets, GPU or Pi dependencies. No second conversation/task implementation or animation dependency was added.

The initial catalog had **41 prompts across five sets**: six core ASR questions/repetition/initials, seven wake/pause/follow-up inputs including silence, fourteen light/music/correction/control inputs, nine stateful ME2 task inputs, and five complex project/progress/correction/speech-stop/task-cancel requests. A subsequent supplemental set is recorded below. Collecting phrases does not imply that tasks execute or physical effects are verified. Catalog text, grouping and reference expectations have one source in recording_lab.py.

Capture flow: one browser-authorized microphone stream feeds MediaRecorder plus a measured level meter. Visual countdown and automatic duration advance each phrase; no audio cue contaminates capture. Captures upload sequentially to `var/recordings/guided/<batch-id>/` with atomic manifests and unique take files. Each take preserves timestamps, expected phrase, scenario/task IDs, duration, actual browser settings, note, hash and completion flag. Retakes preserve originals. A stopped partial take is saved and excluded from default replay; latest complete takes are selected. Review playback is manual and unavailable while recording. Upload failure retains the blob, offers retry/local download, and stops auto-advancing. Saved batches can resume after page refresh. The microphone and meter loop are released when stopped/complete/page exit. No manual transfer is needed on a successful upload.

Privacy/integration: capture has no provider/tool invocation path. Host/Origin loopback checks, a page token, nonce CSP without unsafe-eval, upload size/container/metadata checks, UUID/prompt allowlists and private batch/take permissions protect uploads. No credentials are exposed to the page. The consent covers project storage/university ASR replay; other providers are not automatically authorized. The utility listens only on 127.0.0.1. No model/shared/boot service or existing bridge was started/restarted; existing ME2 and Pi state were untouched.

`recording_lab evaluate` reuses `SpeechClient` and optional canonical `Session`, requires `--max-requests`, validates clip paths/hashes and writes a new report/checkpoints instead of replacing evidence. ASR-only comparison preserves raw transcripts, reference-word edits, WER, decoded input duration and ASR MCP software time. In `--session` mode, input ordering follows scenario groups, and assistant text, task receipts, downstream errors and monotonic trace timings are retained; actions always use explicit mock adapters, never the Spotify configuration/GPIO/Onit. Default reasoning/TTS are mocks. Optional `--live-reasoning`/`--live-tts` require explicit flags, compatible university configuration and the same per-role bounded allowance. Optional live flags were not tested here. Generated reply WAVs are saved when live TTS is explicitly tested. General Onit execution remains separately gated; complex recorded phrases are preparation inputs and are not proof of implemented execution. Mock reasoning cannot establish natural tool-selection accuracy. Direct committed-clip replay bypasses wake/VAD and is not acoustic interruption/AEC verification. Existing CLI/frontend scenarios remain the route for continuous wake/endpoint/interrupt testing.

### What this corpus can and cannot simulate

- The corpus is suitable for same-audio ASR comparisons and for sequential scenario replay. Same-scenario order supports music request → correction → stop; Philippines → Japan time correction; timer → cancellation; reminder → list; website request → progress/correction/speech-stop/task-cancel; plus light changes. The audio evaluator can run the canonical `Session` and mock device/music adapters, with actions isolated from live Spotify/GPIO.
- `--session` submits each clip, waits for its turn to finish, then submits the next. It does not inject an interruption while assistant output is pending. The `speech-stop` recording therefore checks words only, not barge-in timing. Existing deterministic scenarios cover cancellation, stale turns, playback queue clearing and task idempotency independently. Actual full-duplex requires synchronized microphone plus playback-reference audio; this corpus contains no speaker/music playback.
- The evaluator's default `MockLLM` is a generic mock and does not make arbitrary natural-language tool selections. Exact direct Session routes (music, supported lighting phrases and clock forms) can exercise mock effects; broader task tool selection requires a separately bounded live reasoning run. The evaluator's task owner is `MockTaskExecutor`, not the Onit worker. The project-request recordings can verify ASR but cannot demonstrate website creation/progress through Onit. Do not claim general agent or full-duplex support from these clips alone.
- Batch 5 already records task correction (“Use a light theme and add a section about local food”), speech stop while keeping work (“Stop speaking, but keep working on the website”), progress, and explicit task cancellation. These are phrase samples, not concurrent lifecycle evidence. The current `OnitTaskExecutor` does not implement `execute_background`; `Session` therefore awaits its normal `execute` call and receives no Onit phase callbacks. Its worker task is shielded from caller cancellation, while a new Onit job is rejected as `task_busy` if one is still running. Consequently, mock background-task tests prove that the separate mock worker can continue after speech interruption, but neither the recorder nor current Onit path proves that an in-progress Onit task can be updated, resumed by voice, or cancelled cleanly while retaining a receipt. Add a deterministic in-flight task-update/continue/cancel lifecycle scenario and adapt the Onit contract before claiming those behaviors. This work can be developed with text injection and mock tasks without further microphone recordings; acoustic barge-in still needs live audio later.
- The existing task matrix also limits timer slots to 10 seconds, 30 seconds and one minute; the recorded “two minutes” phrase is useful for recognizing the current unsupported-value boundary, not proof that a two-minute timer can execute. Call/message are intentionally unavailable. Natural relative music-volume wording and timer replacement were not recorded in the original sets.

Live microphone/ASR remains deferred. Read current instructions, plan/architecture and experiment 019; git status still reports project untracked in parent repository.
